  • In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp.
  • According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

More showstopping cabbage recipes here.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Recent findings suggest that make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

According to recent reports, while the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

Make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

According to recent reports, when the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam.
  • Recent findings suggest that but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day.
  • In a recent development, in a latest study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

Recent findings suggest that but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These latest forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make said equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

In a recent development, in a latest study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

In a recent development, “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, said in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

According to recent reports, “This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin said. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

In a recent development, according to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

“Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines currently offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

This newly introduced study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

“Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin said. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a major data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Sources indicate that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • It has been revealed that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Sources indicate that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Fresh York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

It has been revealed that for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

It has been revealed that originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, remarked that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Recent findings suggest that part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Upcoming York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

It has been revealed that but while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

In a recent development, A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, states that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Industry observers note that moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to upcoming takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she indicates. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Latest Update: NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone.
  • While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Industry observers note that voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which rolled out half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

According to recent reports, just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, this discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation revealed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons revealed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency unveiled its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that almost all of the major events that changed the trajectory of life on Earth had impossibly tiny beginnings, and the rise of plant life is no exception. Some 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, which eventually evolved into the chloroplast, the specialized organelle that drives photosynthesis in algae and plants. Other eukaryotic cells, of course, took a very different path, giving rise to all animals and, ultimately, the mammalian cells that make up you and me.

Despite the vast evolutionary gulf between them (the two lineages diverged in the middle of the Proterozoic Eon), a new study published in the journal Nature Communications suggests that the cells derived from red algae and mammals still have the capacity to acquire genetic material through a process known as “horizontal gene transfer.”.

Obviously, most gene transfers in nature move from parents to offspring (fittingly named “vertical gene transfer”), but sometimes cells will acquire traits from other individuals, strains, or even entire species. This is seen most commonly in bacteria that share antibiotic resistance genes, or ARGs, creating troublesome antimicrobial-resistant (or drug-resistant) superbugs in the process. However, other fascinating examples exist, including a parasitic worm that can control its host by swapping genes. In their fresh study, a team of scientists led by researchers at the University of Tokyo explored whether a similar process could take place between cells separated by more than a billion years of evolution, resulting in what the researchers call “planimal” cells.

“We wanted to understand whether entire chromosomes could cross the enormous evolutionary divide between algae and animals and whether animal cells could stably maintain and pass on such foreign genetic material to their daughter cells,” University of Tokyo biologist Sachihiro Matsunaga, senior author of the study, remarked in a press statement. “These questions are fundamental to understanding how genetic material can move across species boundaries and contribute to evolution.”.

To investigate this possibility, the authors relied on cells derived from the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, along with mammal cells originating from a hamster. Mirroring the primordial event that gave rise to plant life, the researchers allowed the mammalian cell to engulf the alga, after which—surprisingly—cell fusion produced stable hybrid cells. Armed with advanced imaging and genome sequencing, Matsunaga and his team could track how well host mammalian cells retained this algal DNA over subsequent generations. They found that 16.3 million algal base pairs and intact chromosome sequences from all 20 algal chromosomes were retained, and the algal DNA remained detectable through 155 cell generations.

Industry observers note that “Plants and animals cannot reproduce with each other, so their chromosomes are never combined through mating. Yet, we have succeeded in creating hybrid chromosomes containing genetic material from both an alga and a mammal,” Matsunaga noted. “This demonstrates that even the vast evolutionary divide between plants and animals can be crossed at the level of chromosomes, without reproduction.”.

Industry observers note that the key to the planimal cells’ survival was the epigenetic “gatekeeping” ability of the host cell to essentially silence incorporated foreign DNA. The authors estimate that roughly 96 percent of the algal protein-coding genes were basically offline, but it’s possible that future studies could detect how to flip this gene switch to “on.”.

In a recent development, “Our ultimate goal is to activate these biological pathways and give animal cells some of the unique abilities of plants and algae,” Matsunaga added. “Imagine animal cells that could sustain photosynthesis for long periods, producing oxygen while using carbon dioxide to make useful organic compounds.”.

Industry observers note that so which hot spots should you add to your must-visit list? I asked Yelp to do a deep dive into the most-saved bakeries across America to see which ones people are bookmarking. Here's what came out on top.

It has been revealed that this famed Taiwanese bakery opened its first U.S. outpost earlier this year in Pasadena, California, and has already gone viral for its unique cream cheese-filled bagels and flaky pastries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

In a recent development, more difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

New in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

Food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

There are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

In a recent development, what we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

According to recent reports, the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Good Grips 3-Piece Silicone Utensil Set.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes.

It has been revealed that what we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

What we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No.

In a recent development, what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

According to recent reports, once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

It has been revealed that if steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Industry observers note that whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

It has been revealed that A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

Sources indicate that the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

According to recent reports, with five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That mentioned, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

It has been revealed that high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

It has been revealed that not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

Latest Update: The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

That said, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

To determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Industry observers note that lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

To test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

Industry observers note that the Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

Sources indicate that the Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

Since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for latest detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

Sources indicate that while it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

While I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He claims it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

The Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for newly introduced detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

It has been revealed that because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Recent findings suggest that underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, states that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

The Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Industry observers note that both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

Industry observers note that while I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

According to recent reports, the Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Sources indicate that its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

It also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

Sources indicate that it’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

This one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a newly introduced and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

While shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a big difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s important to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to newly introduced people.

Most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Recent findings suggest that most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

In a recent development, the first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

Sources indicate that the physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

Recent findings suggest that that said, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you plan to scan a wide range of environments.

It has been revealed that in general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how quickly you tire out.

According to recent reports, mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

High-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

Lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That said, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced quickly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

“Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert claims. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”.

In a recent development, lubbert also stated that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

Finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you proposal to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

Depending on who you are, cooking a full Thanksgiving dinner can bring either excitement or complete dread. If you fall into the latter camp, Costco is here to help with its newest offering in the deli department.

Recent findings suggest that laura Lamb of @costcohotfinds shared on social media that the warehouse’s Thanksgiving dinner kit has officially returned for 2026. The prepared meal includes all the holiday essentials, with much of the prep work already taken care of.

Industry observers note that each kit comes with a seasoned half turkey breast over a bed of herbed stuffing, along with Yukon Gold mashed potatoes, green beans, cranberry sauce, and gravy. Costco is pricing the meal at just $3.99 per pound, which works out to around $40 to feed seven to eight people.

It has been revealed that the label includes simple instructions for preparing all the components. The uncooked turkey, naturally, takes the most time. Since it’s placed over the stuffing, the turkey drippings add even more flavor and moisture as it roasts in the oven.

The warehouse keeps this dinner kit pretty consistent from year to year, although one Costco shopper wasn’t as impressed with a particular component this time around. Costco fan and content creator @photogami reports that the gravy is a bit underseasoned and not as good as it was last year. (Thankfully, this problem has a pretty easy solution.).

Lamb also noted that you’ll still need to buy a few extras to round out the meal, like dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. And if you’re a stuffing lover, the amount that comes in Costco’s kit might not be enough for you.

According to recent reports, still, it’s hard to argue with the price and convenience—and members are already eager to pick up a kit for their own holiday celebrations. “Got this last year and it was all absolutely delicious,” one user on Instagram wrote. “Highly recommend.” Another commented, “This is such a great idea for a smaller Thanksgiving!”.

If you want to grab a kit for yourself, blueprint accordingly. All Costco locations are closed on Thanksgiving Day, so you only have a few days to snag one.

Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

Sources indicate that “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Industry observers note that before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

Industry observers note that the conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

Industry observers note that “This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

“Part of the concern here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., mentioned voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul noted.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

Industry observers note that “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they noted, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno remarked, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., mentioned on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

Recent findings suggest that “It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

It has been revealed that “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • Industry observers note that the day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

Industry observers note that the day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

It has been revealed that while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

Recent findings suggest that but getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an important role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

In a recent development, I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

According to recent reports, but for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

In a recent development, smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

Unlike loungers or couches, office chairs require upright support that promotes good posture for your back and neck. They also need to be flexible and mobile enough to move with you throughout a full work day, whether that’s leaning back during a quick break or rolling across the floor to grab something from the printer.

Choosing the right office chair means considering your body type and how long you sit at your computer or gaming desktop on an average day. Check out our list of the best office chairs for support and comfort, plus a few essentials to consider before you make your final decision.

According to recent reports, we researched options across several major online retailers and compared their key specs, design, and adjustable features. We also looked at opinions from reviewers, real-life buyers, and users on online discussion forums such as Reddit. After narrowing our list to a few dozen qualified options, we pared it down further based on price and availability. Regardless of your budget or personal tastes and needs, you should be able to find a comfortable office chair.

According to recent reports, this Branch office chair is modern, with an understated design and solid support features. What sets it apart from other options here is its six points of adjustability. That includes adjustable lumbar support to improve posture and prevent fatigue, and a back that tilts and locks for a more relaxed position.

The chair’s firm, cushioned base is slightly curved at the front and back to support a more natural seated leg position. The seat also adjusts forward and backward.

Considering the customizable settings for comfort and support, this office chair is a far better option than any others at this price point.

The Staples Dexley’s headrest slides up and down and tilts to line up with the back of your head. You can also move the lumbar support to match the curve of your lower back. The seat and back are both mesh, so you'll stay cooler on a long workday than you would in a padded chair.

The Dexley uses a synchro-tilt mechanism, which tips the seat and backrest together when you lean back. A tension knob sets how hard you have to push to recline, and the tilt lock holds the back in one of three positions. The seat height runs from 17.4 to 21 inches, and the armrests move up and down. The seat depth is fixed, though, so you can't slide it forward or back to fit your leg length. Staples claims the chair can support up to 275 pounds over a 5- to 10-hour workday and covers it with a 5-year limited warranty.

Recent findings suggest that the Hon Ignition 2.0 has a lumbar pad that moves up and down the backrest to meet the curve of your lower back. The pad is hard plastic, and a few Amazon reviewers said it pressed into their backs harder than they liked. The seat slides forward and back. If you need extra head and neck support, this office chair is worth a look. The adjustable headrest cradles the back of your head and neck to help prevent strain and fatigue. The chair is covered in a breathable nylon mesh fabric that’s easy to wipe clean.

It has been revealed that other highlights include armrests that adjust in three different directions, plus it offers good lumbar support with adjustable height and width. The office chair also locks in a reclining position for sturdy yet relaxed support.

Sources indicate that most office chair armrests go up and down, and that's it. The Gesture's rotate a full 360 degrees, so they can swing in under your forearms when you're typing and stay there when you lean back to scroll on your phone. The back curves to follow the S-shape of your spine instead of pressing flat against it. Steelcase also built air pockets into the seat cushion, which it indicates ease pressure when you're sitting for hours.

You don't have to stand up or lean over to adjust the Gesture. All the controls sit on the right side of the seat. From there, you can slide the seat forward or back, set how hard you push to recline, or lock the back upright. The recline stops at three positions.

The Gesture holds up to 400 pounds, more than any of our other picks. The weak spot is the lumbar support. It's built into the back and doesn't adjust on this version. If lower-back support is your main concern, our lumbar pick gives you more control for much less.

According to recent reports, A good office chair must be both ergonomic and supportive. Ergonomic design promotes good posture and keeps your body in an optimal position for focusing and working. Ergonomics and good posture go hand in hand with quality lumbar support. Office chairs with good lumbar support feature curved or cushioned backs that align closely with the natural curve of your lower spine, keeping you comfortable and upright for long stretches. Some office chairs have air pumps or adjustable curvatures to tailor the chair closely to your body.

Getting the right fit in an office chair depends on its adjustability. Most swivel and roll chairs have adjustable pneumatic bases that raise and lower the chair so your legs stay at a flat, comfortable level. Along with these basic features, some office chairs have an air pump for customizable lumbar support or attachable cushion straps or neck rests, and height-adjustable armrests that slide side to side.

Industry observers note that office chairs are typically made of polyester, leather, or cloth, plus foam. Most polyester or plastic chairs have lightweight, breathable mesh seats and backs that still offer solid lumbar support. Leather and cloth office chairs are typically cushioned for a bit more give. Foam gently molds to your body and may be more comfortable for your legs and back than mesh office chairs.

It’s the same kind of quality-of-life upgrade you get from buying a washing machine. Once you have one, it’s hard to imagine life without it.

Adding a dishwasher to your home is an key decision, especially since it’s something you’ll be using a few times per week. We also relied on previous Popular Mechanics testing and extensive research to weigh the features that matter most in daily use.

Specifically, we prioritized quiet operation (favoring models under 50 decibels that won’t interrupt a conversation), adjustable racks and foldable tines, and proven cleaning performance. We then cross-referenced these insights with long-term reliability reports to ensure every pick on this list is built to last.

For our most recent upgrade, we revisited the current dishwasher landscape to ensure every recommendation still holds up. We added fresh picks that offer a strong value, smart features, and a great fit for specific needs, like compact kitchens and busy households. We also re-evaluated our existing selections to confirm they remain competitive on price, performance, and availability.

Storage is flexible, too. You get a standard third rack for utensils and other small items, plus a middle rack that adjusts to nine positions to make room for pots below and stemware above. Below, the lower rack has fold-down tines for bulky cookware, making it easier to run a full day’s worth of dishes.
