A 360-Year-Old Manuscript Reveals Galileo May Have Built a Telescope Far Ahead of Its Time

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.
  • In a recent development, in 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities.
  • In a recent development, the account was discovered by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.

In a recent development, in 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities. A powerful colonial official handed him a telescope and demanded a detailed explanation of how it worked. Nearly 360 years later, the account he produced has resurfaced with a remarkable claim: the instrument was made by Galileo Galilei, and its design may be far more advanced than historians previously believed possible for his time.

In a recent development, the account was discovered by Dr. José María Moreno Madrid, a researcher at the University of Limerick’s School of History and Geography in Ireland, while examining a manuscript written by Dominican friar Ignacio Muñoz. Dated 1666 and titled De Tellescopiis Stellarum, the document describes a four-lens telescope that Muñoz identified with the Latin phrase “fabricatum a Galilaeo,” meaning “manufactured by Galileo.”.

The description is unusually precise. Muñoz documented the telescope’s individual components, including its reverse-tapered body and an arrangement of four lenses that allowed distant objects to appear upright. His account describes an erecting eyepiece and convex lenses separated by twice their focal lengths, accompanied by detailed diagrams and drawings that show how the instrument was constructed.

Recent findings suggest that these technical details matter because historical records have generally placed the earliest four-lens telescopes around 1643 to 1645, with their production becoming widespread across Europe beginning in the 1640s. If the instrument really came from Galileo’s workshop, the timeline of telescope development would need to be reconsidered.

In research published in Annals of Science, Moreno Madrid explains what the attribution could mean.

“If, as the text claims, the telescope analyzed was indeed manufactured by Galileo, then the earliest known experimentation with four-lens telescopes would have to be pushed back to 1630 at the latest and credited to him. Moreover, Muñoz’s De Tellescopiis Stellarum would become the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope provenly made by Galileo – and, somewhat paradoxically, it would concern a four-lens telescope rather than the Galilean design that ultimately came to bear his name,” said Dr. Moreno Madrid.

In a recent development, the circumstances surrounding Muñoz’s examination provide another intriguing piece of the story. After traveling from Spain to the Philippines, he became involved in an illicit attempt to establish a newly introduced Dominican religious order and was subsequently exiled to Portuguese India. Hoping to return to Spain, he contacted King Philip IV with a proposal that promised to improve the performance of Spanish fleets operating around the world.

Muñoz offered his nautical innovation in exchange for royal sponsorship of his journey home aboard the Manila Galleon, which traditionally stopped in Newly introduced Spain, a Spanish colonial territory. His proposal, however, attracted suspicion from Antonio Sebastián de Toledo Molina y Salazar, the viceroy of New Spain and Marquis of Mancera.

The viceroy questioned whether Muñoz possessed the scientific knowledge he claimed and worried that the friar was simply trying to persuade the king to pay for his travels. To test his abilities, Mancera presented him with the telescope and ordered him to examine it thoroughly. That assignment produced the technical description Moreno Madrid has now brought to light.

Determining whether Galileo actually manufactured the instrument is more complicated. Although the astronomer famously maintained that he had never sold a telescope and never intended to, very few instruments from his lifetime survive with reliable records of their origins. Of the eight surviving telescopes manufactured during the first half of the seventeenth century, none can be attributed to Galileo beyond dispute. Two preserved in the Museum of Florence have traditionally been credited to him, although that identification is not universally accepted. Galileo also left no technical analyses of his own telescopes.

There is, however, a possible connection between Galileo and the Spanish official who possessed Muñoz’s instrument.

According to recent reports, historical accounts indicate that Galileo presented three telescopes, one large and two smaller instruments, to Philip IV and his wife. He hoped to gain favor with the Spanish court and improve his chances of receiving a substantial reward offered for solving the “problem of longitude,” the longstanding difficulty of determining a ship’s east-west position while navigating at sea.

In a recent development, the optical designs of those three telescopes remain unknown, leaving open the possibility that one was the four-lens instrument described by Muñoz. Moreno Madrid suggests that the Spanish royal family may have later given it to Mancera in recognition of his diplomatic and political achievements.

“I believe that the unambiguous attribution of the telescope in the manuscript, together with the documentary evidence that three telescopes made by Galileo – whose optical configuration remain unspecified – may have been accessible to Mancera through his connections at the Spanish court, at the very least invites consideration of this possibility.”.

No further reference to the telescope appears in Mancera’s surviving correspondence with the Spanish court, making Muñoz’s manuscript the only known document connecting this particular instrument to Galileo.

According to recent reports, moreno Madrid also points to Muñoz’s background in mathematics and astronomy as an important reason to take his technical account seriously. The manuscript describes an optical arrangement absent from existing documentation produced by or associated with Galileo and his contemporaries. Regardless of whether the attribution can ultimately be confirmed, it offers historians a rare opportunity to examine seventeenth-century telescope construction in detail. It also illustrates how these instruments served as prestigious possessions among Europe’s political and scientific elites.

For now, the identity of the telescope’s maker remains an open question, one that Moreno Madrid hopes further discoveries will help resolve.

“It is to be hoped that newly introduced documentary or material evidence will soon emerge to confirm the telescope’s attribution and further enhance our understanding of it.”.

Reference: “De Tellescopiis Stellarum (1666). Was Galileo experimenting with four-lens terrestrial telescopes by 1630?” by José María Moreno Madrid, 12 May 2026, Annals of Science. DOI: 10.1080/00033790.2026.2661195.

  • Physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals.
  • Sources indicate that the experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1.8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals. Their unconventional communication system relied on a moving elevator counterweight and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in the gravitational field.

Sources indicate that the experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1.8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter positioned in a nearby bathroom detected the gravitational changes and decoded a single word: “Gravity.”.

Industry observers note that unlike radio waves and other electromagnetic signals, gravitational fields cannot be blocked by ordinary building materials. This means information carried by changes in gravity could potentially reach places where conventional wireless communication struggles.

It has been revealed that dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ’s School of Mathematics and Physics explained the advantage. “Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” he said. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”.

The communication experiment grew out of an unrelated effort to measure vehicle weights without physical contact. Dr. Andrew Groszek and his colleagues were developing a system that could estimate the mass of trucks and other heavy vehicles by detecting their gravitational attraction.

Industry observers note that “We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr. Groszek said. “Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”.

It has been revealed that the researchers applied that principle to communication by moving a large mass between fixed positions. Each movement altered the gravitational field measured by the detector, allowing the team to encode binary information without transmitting electromagnetic signals.

It has been revealed that although the experiment successfully transmitted information, its data rate was exceptionally low. Professor Andrew White identified the aging elevator as a major constraint.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White stated.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how substantial the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.”.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”.

Recent findings suggest that professor Matthew Davis said the experiment established that information can be deliberately encoded in a gravitational field and recovered by a detector. The achievement demonstrates the underlying physics, although substantial improvements would be needed before the technique could serve as a useful communication system.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely newly introduced way of communicating,” Professor Davis noted. “We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.”.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also modeled how more sensitive quantum sensors might improve the technique. Unlike the classical gravimeter used in the experiment, such sensors could potentially detect weaker gravitational changes at greater distances.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (about 1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”.

Those figures are theoretical projections, not experimentally demonstrated capabilities. Gravity-based communication remains far too slow for practical applications, but more advanced detectors could eventually make it possible to exchange information in environments that radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Reference: “Unblockable communication with gravity” by Andrew J. Groszek, Charles W. Woffinden, Michael D. Harvey, Andrew G. White and Matthew J. Davis, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee0802.

In a recent development, when it comes to keeping your house clean, a reliable vacuum is a must. Vacuums are the quickest and easiest way to tackle dust bunnies, stubborn pet hair, and debris that collect in hidden corners. But not just any vacuum will do.

Finding the right vacuum is often overwhelming when you’re faced with sifting through dozens of upright models, robot vacuums, and more. A vacuum is a big investment, and an uninformed purchase often leads to disappointment if your choice turns out to be too heavy, too cumbersome, or not powerful enough. Plus, you want to pay for features you need without overspending on extras you’ll never use.

Sources indicate that in this guide, we considered upright, cordless, canister, and robotic options from trusted brands, and evaluated them based on research and rigorous testing. We broke down key factors related to functionality, features, and maintenance to help you find the best vacuum, whether you need a pet-friendly option, one that’s powerful enough to clean up after kids, or a budget-friendly model.

More Home Appliances: Best Vacuums for Hardwood Floors • Best Dryers • Best Clothes Steamers.

It has been revealed that to find the best vacuums for every home, we first gathered a lineup of models across a range of brands, price points, and features. We deliberately chose a mix of canister, upright, stick, and robot vacuums to help ensure our selections accommodate different living situations, flooring types, and cleaning needs.

Recent findings suggest that we focused on criteria like performance, ease of use, and versatility. For meaningful results, we ran each vacuum through a series of real-world tests to simulate common messes they’d be likely to come across in everyday life. We tried them on multiple surfaces like low-pile carpet, thick shag rugs, hardwood flooring, and bare concrete, seeing how well the vacuum adjusted to different demands. This also helped us assess suction power and how well the brush roll adapted to each surface type.

It has been revealed that for debris, we chose materials that mimic typical household spills, like crumbled potato chips, popcorn, coffee, and cereal. The different weights and sizes of rubbish gave us a realistic view of how effectively the vacuum could remove the mess.

Recent findings suggest that we also conducted similar tests with the handheld portions and attachments of these vacuums, using crevice tools and motorized brushes on couch cushions, on upholstery, and in tight corners. We noted how easy the tools were to maneuver, and whether they still packed enough power even when detached from the main unit.

By running each vacuum through comprehensive tests, we were able to get a clear picture of their real-world performance, so we could find dependable models for everyday cleaning.

I love using an upright vacuum for heavy-duty cleaning, and the AZ2002 packs the punch you need for tackling messes on carpets, couches, and floors. This model has two brushes: a soft roller brush and a foam-paddled brush. These work in tandem to increase contact with flooring and rugs, and I think that gives the vacuum a significant boost compared to models with just one traditional brush roll. The AZ2002 successfully picked up cat litter, dirt, and crumbs on a textured area rug.

In a recent development, all the cleaning modes are accessible right on the handle, so I was able to swiftly transition between carpet and laminate flooring without having to stop my cleaning session. The LED headlights brought attention to any dirt and gunk I missed during my initial swipes, too.

The AZ2002 also easily converts from an upright to a motorized canister vacuum. I especially liked using this functionality with the powered pet brush for cleaning couch cushions, so I didn’t have to haul the entire vacuum around. The hose and stick attachments extend to clean crevices and curtains, which I normally wouldn’t be able to reach.

The vacuum is on the heavier side, weighing a little over 16 pounds, but because it functions as a canister vac, I'm not too upset about sacrificing a little portability.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Powered Lift-Away Upright Vacuum Review.

I’ve had this vacuum from Shark for six years, and it has proved to be a reliable choice for apartments with hardwood, tile, area rugs, and two cats—so plenty of hair, litter, and dirt to go around.

In a recent development, I appreciate the Rocket for its lightweight build, convenient features, and usability. It transitions between hardwood and carpets using a switch right above the handle, and the base also detaches to become a handheld vacuum. The dustbin capacity is small, but that’s not uncommon for a stick vacuum. I just empty the dustbin whenever it gets too full by using the quick-release button.

The Rocket is easy to move around and underneath furniture, and it comes with useful attachments like a crevice tool, upholstery tool, and anti-allergen dusting brush for sucking up fine particles. The only bump in the road I’ve come across over the years is when I had a really shaggy carpet—the brush roll would often stop rotating and I’d have to untangle any fibers that got stuck.

According to recent reports, you don’t get a ton of new tech with the Rocket, but I’ve found that it performs well on multiple surfaces. It also stores easily, and doesn’t require any hands-on effort emptying a bag or figuring out how to pair the appliance with a compatible app.

Full Shark HV301 Rocket Ultra-Light Corded Stick Vacuum Review.

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser has a tangle-free brush roll, and even after using the vacuum on two large area rugs and hardwood floors, I didn’t find any hair wrapped in the bristles. What I did find, however, was plenty of pet hair, dirt, and dander in the dustbin because the suction power is strong enough to agitate carpet fibers and pick up debris that might not be completely visible.

I use the Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Hand Vacuum on an everyday basis, so I was excited to see that this upright model comes with a dedicated pet hair attachment for the hose wand. I tried it on my couch cushions, and a couple of pushes back and forth removed a majority of the mess. Plus, the canister detaches from the base so you can carry it around as you clean.

In a recent development, the vacuum only has two settings, plush carpet and low carpet/bare floor, so it isn't as versatile as other vacs for different floor types. But I liked being able to manually turn the brush roll on and off with a control switch on the base, which helped me tackle different cleaning tasks.

Industry observers note that as a whole, this vacuum is a great option if you have allergies or pets. The combination canister-upright design adds maneuverability, and the attachments included are helpful for more intricate cleaning. Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Upright Vacuum Review.

It has been revealed that when I think of canister vacuums, Miele comes to mind, and I’m willing to bet I’m not the only one. The brand is known for its powerful, well-designed canister vacuums, and the Classic C1 Turbo Team is, well, a classic.

It has six suction power settings, including options for hard floors, rugs, and even furniture. The floor head has a toggle switch that you can operate with your foot, switching between cleaning carpeting and hard floors easily.

According to recent reports, the hose is long, which I found helpful because I didn’t have to lug the entire vacuum around as I cleaned. The cord is retractable, and the hose is completely detachable, so the C1 stores easily in a closet or laundry room. There’s also a removable component that holds the crevice tool and brushes.

The suction was impressive on low-pile carpets, but we wouldn’t suggest using this model on dense, thick carpets. The floor head also often lost suction during our tests. I particularly liked using this vacuum on furniture—it glided across the seat cushions, and the attachments came in handy for cleaning in between cracks and seams.

This style of vacuum captures dirt and other messes in self-sealing dust bags, so you’ll be able to clean for longer before needing to do any maintenance.

Full Miele Classic C1 Turbo Team Bagged Canister Vacuum Review.

Industry observers note that it might seem like cleaning is my favorite thing to do, given how many vacuums I’m testing regularly, but even I need a bit of a break sometimes. The Roborock Qrevo Series QV 35A has automated the process for me, so my weekly deep cleans don’t take nearly as long.

Recent findings suggest that I have an 850-square-foot apartment, and it took about 30 minutes for the vacuum to map out my entire home. It worked its way over thresholds, across varied floor types, and in tight spaces with ease. I was impressed by how well it differentiated between carpet and hard flooring, so I didn’t have to worry about my area rugs getting wet during the mopping cycle.

It took 61 minutes for the QV 35A to vacuum my entire apartment. It worked around the perimeter first, and then moved in a zigzag pattern around the rest of the interior. There are a few different power options, and I ran it on turbo for most of the cleaning cycle because I have two pets. I felt like the suction power delivered, but it did kill the battery relatively rapidly.

Mopping is equally as satisfying, and it took roughly half the time to do all my laminate floors. The QV 35A automatically refills and empties its water reservoir, so I don’t really have to do anything besides turn it on and let it do its thing.

The robot vacuum attempted to work its way over the legs of my kitchen island chairs, and after a few tries, it got stuck. Obstacle avoidance was mostly accurate otherwise, but I had to manually add a no-go zone in the app so the vacuum avoids this spot in the future.

Full Roborock Qrevo Series QV 35A Robot Vacuum and Mop Review.

Dyson remains a top brand when it comes to cordless stick vacuums, and I’ve personally tested several of its models. The V15 Detect vacuum comes with a laser cleaner to illuminate hidden dirt, dust, and debris on hardwood floors, and this feature has proved to be very useful for me, even in well-lit rooms. The traditional-style cleaner head works well on carpet, and neither head feels lackluster in suction power.

The cordless-to-handheld structure is nice for going from longer cleaning sessions to quick or more detailed cleaning, and I like using the hair screw tool for removing pet fur from couches, cushions, and more. Better yet, there is a built-in dusting and crevice tool that is great for quick cleanups.

Sources indicate that an LCD screen on the handheld portion demonstrates what size of particles you’re cleaning up in real time, along with battery levels and overall cleanliness status. The HEPA filtration is added peace of mind that you’re getting a thorough clean.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

In a recent development, if a corded stick or upright vacuum isn’t the best choice for your home cleaning needs, then check out the LVAC-300 from Levoit. It’s a cordless stick vacuum that switches between hard floors, rugs, and tiles without skipping a beat or losing suction power. According to our tester, the vacuum uses three different modes to take on an array of cleaning jobs like picking up cat litter or fine dust, without spreading material around your floors.

It only weighs a little over 6 pounds, so it’s easy to lift and maneuver, and the vacuum lays completely flat for cleaning under furniture. The LED headlight on the floor head illuminates any lingering messes in areas with less visibility.

It has been revealed that the LVAC-300 is designed with a five-stage HEPA filter with as much efficiency as an air purifier, and it’s also washable and reusable. The dust container releases with the touch of a button, and it empties just as easily.

According to recent reports, we’re keen on the LVAC-300’s handheld vacuum capability and the various attachments it comes with, like a mini motorized brush for couch cushions and beds, and a crevice tool that is slender enough for car seats. A minor inconvenience is that there’s nowhere to store these accessories, which might occasionally interrupt your cleaning session if you have to change tools.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

According to recent reports, we recently added the Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum to our cleaning tool arsenal. It looks like something from the future, but it actually solves a lot of the problems cordless stick vacuums face in the present, namely when it comes to maneuverability and small-capacity dustbins.

The flexible center pole bends at a joint, which made it much easier for our tester to get under furniture and in tight spaces around his apartment. This vacuum uses detection technology to automatically adjust suction power based on the type of flooring and size of mess, so you don’t have to change manually and potentially miss spills or hidden debris. The floor head light helped illuminate dirt better, too.

Another useful feature is the docking station. Once our tester was finished cleaning, he locked the vacuum back onto the base, and it automatically suctioned collected dirt, hair, and dust out of the main dustbin. This doesn’t entirely offset the small dustbin capacity on the vacuum itself, but it’s nice not having to manually empty the receptacle after every clean.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

Recent findings suggest that we have several roundups of vacuums, including cordless stick models and robots. This guide is dedicated to the top overall vacuums we’ve tested, but there are still a few other units worth considering depending on your cleaning needs.

Miele Guard L1: This canister vacuum offers convenience and power for cleaning different floor types. The Classic C1 Turbo Team we recommend above comes with a powered carpet brush, while the L1 does not. It does have longer cable reach and an illuminated display, but the C1 is the better, more affordable selection if you have a mix of surface types in your home.

In a recent development, shark PowerDetect: This is a buy-up version of the Shark PowerDetect Speed we recommend above. It comes with the same flexible hinge for cleaning under furniture and several intuitive features, including automatic suction adjustment and a cleaner head with LED lights for illuminating dirt. With the regular PowerDetect, you get 10 more minutes of run time and one more level of detection (the vacuum can tell when it’s in a corner or up against a wall and ramp up the suction accordingly). But you get more bang for your buck with the Speed.

Many vacuums are available in both corded and cordless models. Corded vacuums offer unlimited run time, but require a nearby outlet. Cordless or battery-powered models are convenient to use, as you can just pick them up and start cleaning, but they have a limited runtime.

The best option for you depends on how you like to clean—do you vacuum your whole house in one go? If so, go for a corded model. Or do you normally clean one room at a time? Then a cordless option might work just fine for your needs.

Sources indicate that different vacuums are better suited for cleaning hard floors or carpeting, and some feature heads that raise or lower to meet the height of the surface you’re vacuuming. If you have a combination of flooring types, you may want to look for a vacuum with multiple heads and attachments, too.

Vacuum brush rolls, or “beater bars,” come in several different styles, and each is made for specific cleaning tasks and flooring. The most common types you’ll see are bristle, soft, and tangle-free. Bristle rolls are designed with stiff, nylon bristles that are ideal for thick carpets because they lift dirt effectively. They are less optimal on delicate surfaces as their harsh structure causes scratches or other damage.

For hardwood floors, or homes with a mix of surfaces, a vacuum with a soft roll brush is what you need. They’re gentle yet efficient, picking up fine particles without scattering. Tangle-free is best for pet owners, since they resist hair wrapping and are easier to maintain.

Some of today’s vacuums feature dual brush rolls, or have detachable vacuum heads for adjusting to different situations.

According to recent reports, capacity refers to how much dust, dirt, and grime the vacuum can hold before the dustbin needs emptying. Bigger capacities are better for larger homes or heavy-duty cleaning, while smaller dustbins are better for compact spaces or low-lift tasks. Upright vacuums typically have a dustbin capacity of 0.75 liters or more, while stick vacs only hold a couple of quarts at a time.

Industry observers note that maneuverability determines how easily the vacuum navigates around furniture, corners, and other obstacles. Features like swivel steering, lightweight builds, and sturdy wheels all contribute to better control. Typically, vacuums with bigger capacity are more difficult to maneuver around, usually due to a combination of size and weight. Striking the right balance between capacity and maneuverability will help you find a vacuum that’s both efficient and easy to handle.

In a recent development, the suction power of vacuums is commonly measured in Pascals (Pa), a unit that gauges pressure, but some brands—including Dyson—list airwatts, or the watts used by the vacuum to move a unit of air through its nozzle, instead. Not all vacuums have their suction power listed, but when comparing different models, keep in mind that high Pa or airwatts equates to more suction power.

Sources indicate that vacuums vary widely in price ranging from as little as $20 to $1,000 or more. Budget-friendly vacuums tend to have less powerful suction and fewer features, and if it’s a cordless model, its battery life will likely be shorter. Premium vacuums, on the other hand, typically have an ergonomic design that’s more comfortable to operate for longer periods, and their suction power is often noticeably better.

While it’s certainly tempting to give up vacuuming all together, a robot vacuum generally isn’t going to be sufficient to keep your home clean. These vacuums are designed for light-duty cleaning, and they simply can’t match the suction power of a full-size vacuum, especially on carpeting. You might be able to get away with using just a robot vacuum if you have a small home, no pets, and solely hard floors, but I think you’d still find yourself needing another vacuum to clean up occasional messes.

Sources indicate that if you have pets, you know that pet hair wreaks havoc on a vacuum. A few passes over a dirty rug, and all of a sudden there’s a wad of hair wrapped around the brush roll, forcing you to stop and untangle it. To avoid problems like this, I highly recommend vacuums designed for pet hair. These models often have anti-tangle brush rolls and good filters, ensuring they capture all the dirt and dander that your furry friends bring into your home.

Industry observers note that while often neglected, vacuum cleaner maintenance is key to keeping your machine running properly and ensuring it will last for years to come. You’ll want to make sure you’re emptying the bag or dustbin as often as recommended, as well as washing or replacing filters. Periodically cleaning the brush roll improves suction power, too.

Some vacuums are easier to maintain than others, and you’ll want to be honest with yourself about how much maintenance you’re willing to do—otherwise, your expensive tool might break sooner than expected.

Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any newly introduced bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

Sources indicate that the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., stated in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

Sources indicate that “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

Recent findings suggest that “Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

According to recent reports, the Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Sources indicate that jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, noted that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors remarked he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely fresh bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

It has been revealed that congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco noted he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

According to recent reports, the House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#100554. This 3D-Printed Robot Runs, Swims, and Climbs Without Any Electronics

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)

This 3D-Printed Robot Runs, Swims, and Climbs Without Any Electronics

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A robot powered entirely by air could offer a latest way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.
  • A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10.6 miles per hour (4.72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.
  • Built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego, the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robot powered entirely by air could offer a latest way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.

A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10.6 miles per hour (4.72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.

Built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego, the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim. Perhaps most remarkably, the entire robot is 3D-printed in one piece using a single material, and it needs no electronics to move.

The breakthrough, described in Science Robotics, takes inspiration from a centuries-old invention, the steam engine. By adapting the way steam engines make efficient use of pressure, researchers found a way to make their soft robot run more than 100 times faster than an earlier version.

Sources indicate that the project began with a much slower machine. In 2022, researchers at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering developed a 3D-printed, air-powered robot that could walk at just 4 centimeters (about 1.6 inches) per second. Described in a 2025 paper in Advanced Intelligent Systems, the original design demonstrated that a robot could move using nothing more than a network of air-filled chambers and valves built directly into its soft body. Its speed, however, was limited by how much air pressure and airflow the internal structures could withstand.

Recent findings suggest that “Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow. We hoped to overcome this limitation, and we were fortunate to find a solution to make the new robot 100 times faster,” noted Yichen Zhai, a former postdoctoral researcher in Professor Michael T. Tolley’s Bioinspired Robotics and Design Laboratory at UC San Diego.

According to recent reports, zhai and Tolley’s team knew that increasing the air pressure could make the robot move faster. Inside the machine, a connected network of chambers, valves, and tubes directs compressed air to move its legs. Making those structures larger and stronger would allow more air to flow through at higher pressures, but there was a catch. At high speeds, the robot could exhaust pressurized air before using much of its remaining energy, wasting the very power needed to keep it running.

The researchers found their solution in the compound steam engine, which extracts more useful energy by allowing steam to expand through multiple chambers rather than releasing it all at once. They incorporated a similar arrangement into the robot, giving compressed air two jobs as it moves through the body. First, it passes through smaller, high-pressure chambers to operate the valves. It then travels into larger, low-pressure chambers, where it drives the legs.

This two-stage system allows the robot to make better use of its compressed air while achieving speeds far beyond those of its predecessor. It also preserves one of the design’s most appealing features: the entire network of moving parts can be printed together without requiring separate electronic controls.

In a recent development, the researchers described the engineering challenge this way, “The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material. We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”.

To see what their creation could handle, the team tested it across concrete, gravel, lawns, mulch, and sand. The robot successfully navigated these different surfaces, ran down stairs, swam in water, and continued functioning underwater. Its ability to move through such varied environments demonstrates what can be accomplished with a relatively simple, flexible design powered entirely by air.

There is still one major limitation. Although the robot operates without electronics, it remains tethered to an external source of compressed air, such as a conventional air compressor. The researchers hope to reduce its air consumption enough that future versions could carry a portable supply, potentially using a small cartridge of compressed air instead. They also want to develop more sophisticated movements that would allow the robot to steer and manipulate objects.

Eventually, inexpensive robots that can be printed in a single piece and operate without electronics could prove useful in places where conventional machines struggle. The researchers envision applications ranging from disaster response and space exploration to scientific reconnaissance in environments with intense radiation or magnetic fields, where electronic equipment may be unable to function.

It has been revealed that reference: “Printing powerful soft robots on a desktop” by Yichen Zhai and Michael T. Tolley, 18 November 2026, Science Robotics. DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aei1264.

The work was funded by the National Science Foundation.

#100553. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)

Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that early Wednesday (Nov.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a fresh space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

According to recent reports, "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe introduced before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

The close-up view highlighted that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

Sources indicate that while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

Sources indicate that by viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker noted.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

In a recent development, some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

It has been revealed that A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker mentioned, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five fresh moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This demonstrated that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

Sources indicate that by 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

According to recent reports, "We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker stated. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Industry observers note that voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker noted. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

A 72-Year-Old Invention Could Be the Key to Unlocking More Powerful Quantum Computers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technology older than the laser is finding latest life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.
  • It has been revealed that A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge.
  • Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a newly introduced amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technology older than the laser is finding latest life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.

It has been revealed that A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying.

Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a newly introduced amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up.

The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications.

In superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference.

That is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading.

In a recent development, existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once.

Sources indicate that another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers.

The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser.

Masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal.

“Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them new life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.”.

To put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets.

The researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency.

In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source.

“We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo.

In a recent development, in testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely.

Sources indicate that the device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits.

Although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also notable in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners.

Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries.

According to recent reports, reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, S. Onoda, T. Ohshima, J. Isoya, Hiroki Takahashi and Yuimaru Kubo, 16 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79021-7.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter.
  • In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Massive Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

According to recent reports, first, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

In a recent development, instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

It has been revealed that then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Major Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

According to recent reports, still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

Latest Update: Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day.
  • President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.
  • Recent findings suggest that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

Recent findings suggest that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

It has been revealed that vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

According to recent reports, "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself remarked so last night.".

According to recent reports, trump has mentioned that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president remarked Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

According to recent reports, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

It has been revealed that the situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

In a recent development, trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

According to recent reports, trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "swiftly.".

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

Industry observers note that “With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.

#100541. American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it
