American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Sources indicate that the February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that the February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

“Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

Industry observers note that but at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

It has been revealed that the Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and rolled out a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and upgrade climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

But as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she claims. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

It has been revealed that courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

According to recent reports, the Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, claims Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

Since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

“When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” says Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, notes Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

University of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

The effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

“When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin says. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

In 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” says Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

But the thing that really stood out, Young claims, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

Recent findings suggest that so, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

In a recent development, after the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences announced a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed plans to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

“Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” states Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

While private funding can be a lifeline, Young claims, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

According to recent reports, in 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would concern one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

According to recent reports, but in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

“Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

In July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

In a recent development, the loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary claims. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a new group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

Vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. At the moment, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

When the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

In a recent development, while the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell says. It aims to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” claims Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

“I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” says Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Recent findings suggest that although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm states. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

Recent findings suggest that in April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp says. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

Industry observers note that however, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” notes environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a latest set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp claims.

Industry observers note that the American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

According to recent reports, AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” states Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

According to recent reports, AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones notes. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

The Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

Industry observers note that “It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” says Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

Climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” claims Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

In February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a new website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis says.

In a recent development, nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

It has been revealed that “We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is key,” Janis indicates. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

Sources indicate that at the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, indicates colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis claims, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

Even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining latest ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” claims Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

To Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. New bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she says, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

Powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

It has been revealed that janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

However, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

At the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a new science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” claims Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

They have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

“If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey says. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.

Tech Report: What do cadaver dogs smell when they find a buried body?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a pilot study, three cadaver dogs and an electronic nose searched the same grave to see how the dogs’ alerts lined up with the device’s readings.
  • When a cadaver dog lies down over a patch of ground, a search team treats it as the word of an expert.
  • Handlers train the dogs on bone and fluid from decomposing bodies, but the exact chemicals a dog responds to are still unknown.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a pilot study, three cadaver dogs and an electronic nose searched the same grave to see how the dogs’ alerts lined up with the device’s readings.

When a cadaver dog lies down over a patch of ground, a search team treats it as the word of an expert. The expert can’t explain its reasoning, though.

Handlers train the dogs on bone and fluid from decomposing bodies, but the exact chemicals a dog responds to are still unknown.

Over two months, an Australian research team tested three police dogs and a handheld electronic nose at the same grave.

The dogs located the grave consistently after researchers probed the soil, and the electronic nose picked up stronger signals after probing.

The study rests on a single buried donor and three dogs, so the authors call it a pilot.

Amber Brown, now at the University of North Florida, conducted the research while completing her doctorate at the University of Technology Sydney.

Maiken Ueland, who directs the forensic research site where the body was buried, supervised it, with co-authors at the University of Windsor in Canada and in China.

“We don’t know exactly what they are smelling – whether it’s a single compound or a combination of compounds,” Ueland said.

“The electronic nose can provide greater certainty during training by showing whether decomposition odor is present in an area, including when a dog does not alert.”.

Industry observers note that the body belonged to a 79-year-old man who donated it to research. Five days after his death in March 2020, staff buried him about 2 feet (60 centimeters) down in a 12-acre (4.9-hectare) forest plot in western Sydney.

Three empty graves were dug the same day so the dogs couldn’t simply react to disturbed soil.

Sources indicate that the grave then sat untouched for 98 days, long enough to match the standard definition of a long-term missing person. Searches ran on six days between July and September.

That is a Sydney winter, with daily averages between 48°F and 57°F (9°C and 14°C), when buried bodies give off less odor.

In a recent development, on five of the six search days, the team pushed a probe into the grave at 14 points to let trapped gas escape. Soil holds the chemicals of decay the way a sponge holds water, and a probe hole opens a path out.

It has been revealed that the dogs came from the New South Wales Police Force canine unit. Two were English springer spaniels, aged three and seven and a half, and one was a four-year-old Labrador retriever.

The youngest had about a year of experience and the oldest about six.

Recent findings suggest that none had worked a buried body before. Each dog was released off leash about 500 feet (150 meters) from the grave, from a different direction each visit, and alerted by lying down or barking.

The handlers didn’t know where the grave was on the first visit, but the head trainer did, and watched from a distance to rule on each alert.

The electronic nose, called NOS.E, carries five gas sensors tuned to the chemical families that buried bodies release, such as alcohols and compounds containing nitrogen or sulfur.

Before each dog ran, a researcher walked it over the grave with its intake about 6 inches (15 centimeters) above the ground. An empty control grave 16 feet (5 meters) away was sampled the same way.

After probing, every dog tested alerted over the donor’s upper torso, where the device registered its strongest readings.

Over the whole trial, the sensors for nitrogen and sulfur compounds and for alcohols responded most.

Industry observers note that the two younger dogs each gave a false alert during searches before probing. The oldest dog never gave a false alert.

Once the grave was probed, no dog missed it and none alerted in the wrong place.

Recent findings suggest that air samples sent to a lab confirmed the same chemical families were present on every search day. They surged after heavy rain and a warm spell around days 126 and 147.

With so few alerts to compare, the statistics could not confirm a link between sensor strength and correct alerts, though correct alerts tended to come with higher readings.

Brown stated the device could give trainers another way to check whether a dog’s alert coincides with a chemical signal consistent with decomposition.

“For younger dogs in particular, the technology could help trainers determine whether a dog is genuinely responding to decomposition odor or being influenced by another cue,” she mentioned.

In a recent development, the device is not meant to replace the dogs. A dog covers ground rapidly and smells things no sensor array can, while the device uses sensors that respond to broad groups of chemicals.

On the last day the probe punctured the remains, and every sensor fired at once on gases a normal search would never release.

One donor, buried at one depth in one season, is the whole dataset.

The dogs may have learned where the grave was over six visits, even though they started from different spots each time.

And the device has not been tested against other soils, deeper burials, or mixed smells, so it is not ready for a real search.

Whether a dog alerts to a single compound, a mix, or a concentration is still the open question.

Ueland’s team plans a larger study with several donors and more dogs over repeated visits. The hard part, she noted, will be keeping the dogs and handlers from learning the sites.

Until that study runs, the pairing has been tried on one grave, and there the sensors and the dogs agreed.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

#100539. An armored amphibian hunted like a shark 237 million years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1136 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

An armored amphibian hunted like a shark 237 million years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two fossils from southern China reveal an armored amphibian that lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago.
  • According to recent reports, no living amphibian is known to spend its entire life in the open ocean.
  • Yet in the Late Triassic, a flat, armored amphibian about 2½ feet (75 centimeters) long lived on the sea floor at least 19 miles (30 kilometers) from the nearest land.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two fossils from southern China reveal an armored amphibian that lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago.

According to recent reports, no living amphibian is known to spend its entire life in the open ocean. For most, seawater draws moisture out through their permeable skin.

Yet in the Late Triassic, a flat, armored amphibian about 2½ feet (75 centimeters) long lived on the sea floor at least 19 miles (30 kilometers) from the nearest land.

Two nearly complete skeletons from southern China provide the first evidence of an amphibian that lived entirely at sea.

The researchers named the species Gerrothorax maritimus. The name maritimus means “of the sea.”.

Their case rests on where the bones lay and what they are made of, plus a suit of armor the animal’s freshwater ancestors already wore.

The fossils were studied by Lipin Diao of the Geological Museum of Guizhou, Ryosuke Motani of the University of California, Davis, and Da-yong Jiang of Peking University, with two colleagues.

“If you think about today’s amphibians, this animal is unusual because it’s substantial,” Motani noted.

“It’s probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what’s different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky.”.

Local fossil collectors dug the skeletons out of a quarry in Guanling County, Guizhou Province, in 2004.

According to recent reports, the bones went to the Geological Museum of Guizhou in 2022, when it opened as the province’s official fossil repository. The rock around them is about 237 million years old.

According to recent reports, the same bed has produced large ocean-going ichthyosaurs, animals of the open sea. In the Late Triassic, this rock was the floor of a gulf about 125 miles (200 kilometers) from any large landmass.

The bones argue against a carcass that drifted out from a river. The larger skeleton still has its fingers in place, and fingers are among the first parts a dead four-legged animal loses at sea.

“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” mentioned Motani, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.

“But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived.”.

It has been revealed that strontium is a metal that animals take in with their water and build into bone. The mix of its forms differs between the open ocean and water that drains off land.

The team measured that mix in dense bone from both skeletons and in the rock around them.

The bone values were close to the global seawater value of the time. The surrounding rock read higher, closer to the older rocks of the nearby land.

The two skeletons also agreed with each other far more closely than the rock samples did, which the authors read as a living body controlling its own chemistry.

In an interview with Earth.com, Motani said the strontium result needed little interpretation.

“I was surprised to see a clean result, which did not require a lot of interpretations to say A or B,” he said.

Amphibians breathe and drink through their skin, and that’s what fails them in the ocean, Motani said.

A few living species can tolerate brackish water, and some can even withstand brief exposure to seawater.

“This wonderful device, however, does not do its job in sea water and instead works against the animal,” Motani told Earth.com.

Gerrothorax had a way around that long before it reached the sea. Its back was covered in a pavement of bony plates about an inch across and less than a fifth of an inch thick.

It has been revealed that A second layer of bony rods and small plates protected the belly. The lineage also kept internal gills into adulthood, which most living amphibians lose.

In a recent development, the researchers propose that the armor limited water exchange through the skin. If so, the animal may have taken in water by drinking seawater and shed excess salt through its gills, much as marine fish do.

The armor evolved in fresh water as protection from predators, Motani noted, and happened to be the right equipment for a later move into the sea.

“There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonize the sea – the body armor,” he said.

Industry observers note that the larger skeleton is 29 inches (74 centimeters) long as preserved. The skull is only about 5 inches (13 centimeters) long but close to 10 inches (25 centimeters) wide. The armored back reaches about 11 inches (29 centimeters) across.

It has been revealed that the animal’s hind legs are longer than its front legs. The authors read that as a sign it breathed with gills rather than lungs, since lung-breathing sea animals usually need longer front legs to stay balanced in the water.

The throat bones are heavily built, as strong as those of sharks that feed by suction. So the team pictures a flat animal resting on the bottom, like a wobbegong carpet shark, and swallowing whatever swam too close.

“They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in,” Motani mentioned.

The salt-handling system and the feeding style are inferences from bone, since no soft tissue survived.

Nobody knows whether these ancient amphibians had permeable skin like a frog’s. Nor do the fossils say whether Gerrothorax maritimus laid eggs or gave birth to live young, and amphibian eggs do poorly in salt water.

The species also lived in a greenhouse world, much warmer than today’s.

Even a return to those temperatures would probably not open the sea to modern amphibians, the authors wrote, because most of them lose their gills as adults.

Land vertebrates have colonized the ocean roughly 70 times, and this is the only amphibian lineage known to have gone all the way.

Asked by Earth.com where more marine amphibians might turn up, Motani pointed to Triassic marine shales laid down in the tropics of the time.

According to recent reports, the best bet, he said, is near where the ancient Panthalassa and Tethys oceans met. Those rocks are where this one came from, and where China’s Triassic marine reptiles keep appearing.

Whether Gerrothorax maritimus was alone in the sea, or the first of several armored relatives to make the crossing, is the question those shales will have to answer.

Until a second one turns up, the whole case for a marine amphibian rests on two skeletons from one quarry.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

#100538. Mangrove forests are using washed up ocean weeds to build their soil and fight rising sea levels

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1287 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Mangrove forests are using washed up ocean weeds to build their soil and fight rising sea levels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2.
  • In a recent development, mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them.
  • Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2. Unfortunately, they are losing the race against rising sea levels.

In a recent development, mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them. To survive, the ground under the trees has to build up as fast as the ocean rises. A latest study finds that dead seagrass helps that happen.

Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.

Sources indicate that he then waded in to see what the tide had left. Much of it was dead seagrass and macroalgae, the debris that scientists call “marine wrack.”.

When seagrass washes into a mangrove forest, it adds material to the forest floor and traps carbon that would otherwise warm the climate.

An isotope model estimated that seagrass supplied between 36 and 53 percent of the soil carbon near the surface at his two sites, according to FIU. It has not closed the gap, because the sea there is rising at least twice as fast as the ground.

Montenegro and a field partner worked at two sites in Biscayne National Park, on the Atlantic coast of Florida. The paper calls them BISC-1 and BISC-2. They lie about 5 miles (8 kilometers) apart, in a narrow band of forest along the shore.

BISC-1, the southern site, sits just south of the mouth of the Homestead Military Canal and east of the L-31E levee, built in 1966.

BISC-2 sits near the mouth of the Black Creek Canal, in the Cutler Wetlands, where roads and urban development run beside the shore.

Levees and roads stop these mangroves from moving inland, and little river sediment reaches them.

The National Park Service set up both monitoring stations with a surface elevation table, an instrument that records small changes in ground height from a fixed benchmark.

The readings run from February 2011 at BISC-1 and January 2012 at BISC-2 through September 2024. BISC-1 has 25 rounds of measurements and BISC-2 has 23.

Sea level in the bay is rising about 8.5 millimeters (0.33 inch) a year, based on data from the NOAA tide gauge at Virginia Key.

The ground at BISC-1 rose about 2.1 millimeters (0.08 inch) a year, and the ground at BISC-2 rose about 3.9 millimeters (0.15 inch).

That left BISC-1 about 6.4 millimeters (0.25 inch) short each year. Below the surface, the land at BISC-1 sank 0.7 millimeters a year and the land at BISC-2 sank 0.4.

In a recent development, hurricane Irma hit the area in 2017. Elevation at both sites had climbed sharply until 2014, declined from 2014 to 2019, and has risen steadily since 2018, possibly from fresh plant growth and sediment moved by the storm, the authors wrote.

In a recent development, yearly gains are 1.1 millimeters higher at BISC-1 and 2.2 higher at BISC-2 than in the last regional synthesis. Other research has warned that Florida’s mangroves may end up underwater as seas climb.

It has been revealed that montenegro made 23 monthly wrack surveys between May 2022 and May 2024. He and his partner marked three lines at each site, each one 66 feet (20 meters) long, and stopped at the shoreline, at 33 feet and at 66 feet.

At every stop they laid down a frame of about 11 square feet (1 square meter), wrote down how much seagrass, macroalgae, plastic, wood and mangrove litter lay inside it, and measured the pile with a meter stick. Then they photographed it.

It has been revealed that researchers usually study wrack on beaches, FIU said, since they can walk up to it or see it from satellites. Neither works well under a mangrove canopy.

For the decomposition test, the team filled nylon bags with about 5 grams of red mangrove leaves or the seagrass Thalassia testudinum.

They left the bags on the soil and collected them after six and 12 months, then repeated the experiment for a second year.

According to recent reports, the surveys also caught a regional event. Sargassum, a brown macroalga, reached its highest level on the plots in March 2023, the same month the University of South Florida‘s satellite system reported a peak across the region.

It has been revealed that south Florida’s mangroves are generally thought to build soil from their own leaves, wood and roots, according to FIU. The team pulled soil cores 4 inches (10 centimeters) deep during four sampling rounds and removed the roots where possible.

They then measured stable isotopes, forms of carbon and nitrogen that differ between plant sources, and ran a statistical model that compared the soil with red mangrove and seagrass tissue.

In the top 0.8 inch (2 centimeters), the seagrass share ranged from 36.1 percent at the innermost point of BISC-1 to 53 percent at the same point of BISC-2.

BISC-2, in the Cutler Wetlands, received more than 3.4 times as much wrack as BISC-1 at 66 feet inland, and its ground rose fastest. The seagrass share fell lower down the cores, likely because roots add more material at depth.

Where more wrack piled up, seagrass in the bags broke down more slowly at both sites, and mangrove leaves did the same at BISC-2.

Past measurements at the stations recorded single wrack deposits adding between 0.07 and 1.8 inches (1.78 and 46.38 millimeters) to the surface.

According to recent reports, montenegro knew both habitats before the project began. As an FIU undergraduate he worked in a seagrass lab that studied water quality damage, and he later measured mangrove elevation with the National Park Service.

“We know seagrass ecosystems are very sensitive to water quality,” he said in the FIU release. Losing those meadows, he added, would mean “losing a huge contributor to mangrove resilience.”.

The bay is one where climate stress has already changed the water. Mangroves worldwide also face a triple threat to their survival, and rising seas may push some forests to release stored carbon.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that management and restoration efforts should consider strategies that protect the route that carries wrack from seagrass beds into the forests. Montenegro called mangroves and seagrass “puzzle pieces that make our community whole.”.

The study covers two sites in one national park, and the elevation rates carry wide error margins, plus or minus 2.6 millimeters a year at BISC-1 and 3.2 at BISC-2.

Seasonal wrack volume tracked surface elevation change at both sites, but it revealed no clear relationship with the soil accumulation measured above marker layers.

The authors wrote that wrack volume alone was not driving those patterns, and proposed slower decay and added peat as the route.

Their model also used only two sources, red mangrove and Thalassia testudinum, so it did not separate the macroalgae found on the plots.

Water depth has climbed sharply at both sites since 2019, and the authors warned that longer flooding could eventually starve roots of oxygen.

The National Park Service funded the work under agreement P21AC11346-00, and two of the four authors, Kevin Whelan and Michelle Prats, work for its South Florida and Caribbean monitoring network.

Recent findings suggest that montenegro finished his Ph.D. earlier this year and now works in the Department of Environmental Resources Management for Miami-Dade County, on the same coast where he once loaded a canoe before sunrise.

The full study was published in the journal Estuaries and Coasts.

#100536. In 1969, lightning struck Apollo 12 twice during launch, but the crew reached the Moon and brought back a camera tied to a germ myth

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1116 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

In 1969, lightning struck Apollo 12 twice during launch, but the crew reached the Moon and brought back a camera tied to a germ myth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lightning hit Apollo 12 twice in its first minute in 1969.
  • The Apollo 12 moon mission lifted off at 11:22 a.m.
  • Sources indicate that lightning had struck the rocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lightning hit Apollo 12 twice in its first minute in 1969. The crew still landed next to Surveyor 3, whose camera later sparked controversy.

The Apollo 12 moon mission lifted off at 11:22 a.m. EST on November 14, 1969, into a dark, rainy sky over Florida. Thirty-six seconds later, the commander saw a bright flash, and many of the spacecraft’s electronics went offline.

Sources indicate that lightning had struck the rocket. Sixteen seconds after that, a second event knocked out the spacecraft’s guidance system.

The crew still landed on the Moon five days later, right next to a robotic probe that had been sitting there since 1967.

What they brought back from that probe started a story that has never quite gone away: that Earth germs had survived on the Moon.

The crew was commander Charles “Pete” Conrad, command module pilot Richard Gordon and lunar module pilot Alan Bean. Their mission was NASA’s second Moon landing, four months after Apollo 11.

Later crews carried living cargo on purpose, like the tree seeds an Apollo astronaut flew around the Moon in 1971.

A NASA photo reveals a bolt between the clouds and the ground 36.5 seconds after liftoff, when the vehicle was about 6,000 feet up. The first event took the spacecraft’s three power-generating fuel cells offline.

Industry observers note that the Saturn V rocket that was guiding the launch was not affected and kept flying normally. The spacecraft on top of it was another matter.

In a recent development, in Mission Control, a young engineer named John Aaron was watching the spacecraft’s systems. His data turned to garbage during both events.

It has been revealed that aaron had seen similar readings in a test a year earlier. He concluded that a unit called the Signal Conditioning Equipment had suffered some upset and gone offline, and that a seldom-used switch needed to be moved from Normal to Auxiliary.

According to recent reports, he told Flight Director Gerry Griffin, and the call went up to the crew through capcom Gerald Carr. Bean remembered that the switch was on his panel and flipped it. Several seconds later, Aaron had good data on his screen again.

Once Conrad understood what had happened, he radioed Houston: “I think we need to do a little more all-weather testing.”.

For about two and a half hours in Earth orbit, the astronauts and Mission Control checked that every system still worked. Then Carr told them they were go to leave for the Moon.

On November 19, Conrad and Bean landed the lunar module Intrepid in the Ocean of Storms, about 950 miles west of the Apollo 11 site.

They came down about 535 feet from Surveyor 3, an uncrewed NASA lander that had been on the Moon since April 1967. It is the only time Apollo astronauts landed near another spacecraft and touched it.

On their second moonwalk, on November 20, the two men walked into the 650-foot-wide Surveyor Crater. They cut off the probe’s 17-pound TV camera and also collected its motorized scoop, pieces of cable, aluminum tubing and glass.

Engineers wanted the camera to see how its gears, motors, optics, metals and lubricants had held up.

Scientists were most interested in the cable, because biological organisms had been trapped inside it, and they wanted to know if any had survived two and a half years on the Moon.

In a recent development, after splashdown, the camera went to NASA’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston. Sampling for microbes began on January 8, 1970.

Recent findings suggest that A team took 33 samples from 11 locations inside the camera body. One sample, a bit of polyurethane foam used as insulation between the aluminum plates of a circuit board, grew a colony of Streptococcus mitis, a bacterium that commonly lives in the human mouth.

The result was published in 1971. It gave rise to the idea that Earth bacteria had survived the vacuum and the extreme temperatures of the Moon, and that idea has circulated ever since.

The broader question is still studied today, as in research on whether Earth microbes can survive in hidden pockets on the Moon.

According to recent reports, decades later, John Rummel of East Carolina University, Judith Allton of NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Don Morrison reviewed the case. They tracked down the 16mm films of the sampling and watched them.

According to recent reports, their review, now hosted by NASA, lists several problems. No viable microbes were found in 10 of the 11 sampling locations inside the camera, or in 32 of the 33 samples.

None were found in the Surveyor cables or in any Apollo lunar samples, and a test camera that had stayed on Earth never yielded S. mitis.

S. mitis is not a spore former, and microbes like it are much more vulnerable to heat, even in a vacuum. NASA’s Manned Spacecraft Center, now Johnson Space Center, estimated that the camera reached a maximum temperature of about 158 degrees Fahrenheit (70 degrees Celsius).

It has been revealed that there was also no negative control to check whether the sampling itself added microbes. And S. mitis was one of the organisms found on the crew during routine microbial testing.

The films showed technicians in short-sleeved scrubs, with their arms exposed. Just before the foam was sampled, one worker leaned his upper body into the laminar-flow hood and examined the side of the camera where the foam was.

Morrison concluded that his breath could have contaminated the foam. Because the foam was the last sample taken, nobody could check whether nearby surfaces had been contaminated too.

“The general scene does not lend a lot of confidence in the proposition that contamination did not occur,” Morrison wrote.

The review does not prove where the bacterium came from. What it shows is that the claim of survival on the Moon rests on a single sample taken under weak controls.

The authors used the case as a warning for future missions that bring material back from Mars and other worlds.

It has been revealed that contamination should be avoided but anticipated, and a microbial inventory should be taken before launch. Other scientists have since proposed a Moon lab to screen samples for alien microbes.

It has been revealed that their summary also admitted something about the story’s staying power. Just because scientists do not believe it, they wrote, does not mean it is going to go away.

The information was obtained from NASA’s account of the Apollo 12 launch, its mission summary and the review of the Surveyor 3 microbe claim.

Tech Report: Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that former Maine Gov.
  • Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once noted he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.
  • The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once noted he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

It has been revealed that dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

Industry observers note that “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, remarked in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

According to recent reports, lePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent Fresh England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Sources indicate that golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Recent findings suggest that dunlap initially debuted his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

A meteorite older than Earth crashed through a Texas woman’s roof and landed near her daughter’s bed

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite that pierced a home in Spring, Texas is now on free display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.
  • According to recent reports, on the afternoon of March 21, 2026, Sherrie James heard a thunderous boom at her home in Spring, Texas, north of Houston.
  • Eight months later, that rock is on display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science, in a free exhibition called Fall To Earth that opened on November 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 4.5-billion-year-old meteorite that pierced a home in Spring, Texas is now on free display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science.

According to recent reports, on the afternoon of March 21, 2026, Sherrie James heard a thunderous boom at her home in Spring, Texas, north of Houston. A rock from space had just come through her roof.

Eight months later, that rock is on display at the Houston Museum of Natural Science, in a free exhibition called Fall To Earth that opened on November 6.

On the day it fell, it pierced an upstairs bedroom and came to rest near her daughter’s bed. It was a meteorite about 4.5 billion years old, dating back to the birth of the solar system.

In a recent development, james was not the only one who noticed. People across Texas heard a low boom and felt their houses shake, under clear skies, according to the museum.

NASA’s analysis says the meteor became visible 49 miles above Stagecoach, northwest of Houston, at 4:40 p.m. Central Daylight Time. It moved southeast at about 35,000 miles per hour and broke apart 29 miles above Bammel, just west of Cypress Station.

According to recent reports, the space rock that entered the atmosphere weighed about a ton and measured about 3 feet across, NASA estimates. When it broke apart, it released energy equal to 26 tons of TNT. That created a pressure wave that reached the ground and caused the booms.

More than 180 eyewitnesses reported the fireball, from as far away as Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin and Rockport, the museum remarked.

According to NASA, the Geostationary Lightning Mappers on the GOES weather satellites also detected it, and Doppler weather radar showed meteorites falling to the ground between Willowbrook and Northgate Crossing.

Radar has helped track falls before, as researchers showed when they found that weather radar systems can detect meteorite falls.

Industry observers note that at first, nobody knew what had hit the house. The Ponderosa Fire Department initially looked into whether the object might be debris from an aircraft.

In a recent development, its unusual weight and appearance soon pointed to something else. Most of the original space rock burned up before it reached the ground, but some pieces survived.

By late October 2026, 19 meteorite fragments had been recovered around the Houston area, according to the museum.

Researchers at Rice University have proposed naming the meteorite “Houston” as part of its formal classification, which still needs approval from the Meteoritical Society.

It is not the first time a meteorite has hit a home in the United States. A similar rock crashed into a man’s house in Georgia.

Within 24 hours of the fall, experts and enthusiasts were finding small chunks on public property, Rice University remarked. That is rare: meteorites seldom land in a major city, and samples are seldom collected so soon after landing.

It has been revealed that rice scientist Bidong Zhang walked 23,000 steps searching but found no samples himself. Two other searchers, David Gonzales and Marc Fries, found several pieces and donated them to Rice.

Those samples became the first meteorite tested and catalogued by Zhang’s upcoming Rice Astromaterials Research and Exploration lab, known as RARE.

Sources indicate that the analysis confirmed that the Houston meteorite is a chondrite, a type of stony meteorite. Its oxygen isotopes matched what scientists call high-grade H chondrites.

According to recent reports, but there was a mystery. Chondrites usually contain small round grains called chondrules, and the Houston meteorite had none.

Industry observers note that the scientists found clues in a mineral called feldspar, which was in an unusual sodium-rich form. That suggests the rock was heated to nearly 1,100 degrees Celsius (about 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit) while it was still part of its parent asteroid, hot enough to melt the chondrules.

Sources indicate that at some point after that, a high-speed impact likely broke up the asteroid and set the meteorite free. “We think this meteorite was impacted in space,” Zhang remarked. “It truly is a unique specimen.”.

Industry observers note that some results are still unexplained. The levels of one oxygen isotope varied within the samples, when scientists would normally expect them to be fairly consistent, and the team claims more work is needed.

The museum calls it one of the most remarkable, documented meteorite falls in recent Texas history. Because the rock dates to the birth of the solar system, it offers scientists a rare chance to study material older than Earth itself.

“A 4.5-billion-year-old fragment of our solar system’s original formation crashed through the roof of a Houston-area home,” noted Carolyn Sumners, vice president of astronomy at the Houston Museum of Natural Science. “That’s not something you expect to happen in your own neighborhood.”.

James sees it in a more personal way. “That little thing has traveled by planets and stars, there’s no telling how far it’s come,” she said. “So, it’s very exciting. I just feel blessed it came to see me.”.

Fall To Earth is free and open to the public at the museum, at 5555 Hermann Park Drive in Houston.

The information was obtained from the Houston Museum of Natural Science, Rice University and NASA’s fireball report.

Industry News: Dust left by an exploded star holds clues to its final hours

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb’s fresh view of Cassiopeia A reveals how dust from a supernova can preserve clues to what happened inside the star before it exploded.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope shows a cloud of debris left behind by an exploded star.
  • Bright orange strands form a loose ring, with wisps of green along the edges and patches of pale blue scattered through the cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb’s fresh view of Cassiopeia A reveals how dust from a supernova can preserve clues to what happened inside the star before it exploded.

Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope shows a cloud of debris left behind by an exploded star.

Bright orange strands form a loose ring, with wisps of green along the edges and patches of pale blue scattered through the cloud.

The debris stretches about 10 light-years across.

This is Cassiopeia A, the expanding wreckage of a massive star.

The light from its explosion reached Earth more than three centuries ago.

Astronomers are now using dust in the wreckage to investigate a much shorter span of time, possibly just a few hours in the life of the star.

Cassiopeia A lies about 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

It has been revealed that from Earth, the debris appears roughly circular. Within that outline are strands, knots, and clouds of material that took different paths to get there.

It has been revealed that some came from deep inside the star and were hurled into space when it exploded. Other material had already escaped while the star was alive.

One of the features astronomers examined is a structure nicknamed the Green Monster.

It contains dust rich in magnesium silicates and traces back to material shed before the explosion. Two other regions contain debris expelled in the blast.

Sources indicate that one is dominated by silica dust and the other by carbon dust. A single image brings those different pieces of the star’s history into view.

In a recent development, as the blast expanded, it pushed into gas around the star. That encounter produced a second shock wave, called a reverse shock, that traveled back through the outward-moving debris.

As the shock encounters clumps of material, it heats them.

Warm dust gives off infrared light, which Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument can detect.

The orange, green, and blue in the image represent infrared light rendered in colors our eyes can see.

The shapes are what first draw the eye, but the chemistry comes from examining how the dust emits light at different wavelengths.

According to recent reports, different kinds of grains leave different signatures. With Webb, astronomers can examine individual clumps that would have blurred together in earlier observations.

Some of those clumps are roughly the size of our solar system.

Late in a massive star’s life, nuclear fusion can take place in several layers at once.

One layer may be hot enough to fuse oxygen while another, farther out, fuses carbon. Material circulates within each of these layers.

Under some conditions, that motion can carry material across the boundary between them until the layers begin to mix. Astronomers call this a shell merger.

A team led by Tea Temim of Columbia University found signs of that mixing in dust across much of Cassiopeia A.

The Webb observations build on X-ray measurements from NASA’s Chandra observatory and the Japan-led XRISM mission.

Together, the observations support the idea that the oxygen- and carbon-burning layers were already mixing when the star’s core collapsed.

That process may have begun mere hours before the explosion.

NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope helped the team decide where to look.

In a side-by-side comparison of Spitzer and Webb images, the older view catches the broad sweep of the glowing debris.

Sources indicate that webb resolves that same patch into narrow threads and individual knots. That difference matters when two clumps close together in the sky contain different kinds of dust.

By studying them separately, astronomers can trace where those differences occur across the remnant.

Some of the material scattered by supernovae can later become part of other stars and planets.

If two layers mixed before the blast, they could change the mixture of elements the explosion sent into the galaxy.

The dust still glowing in Cassiopeia A gives astronomers a way to connect what the star released with what was happening deep inside it just before it came apart.

Breaking: Weight-loss drugs have become more common, but not everyone has access

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study of more than half a million privately insured adults found that where patients received care was linked to whether they filled a prescription for weight-loss drugs.
  • Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold as Wegovy and Zepbound, and the two weight-loss drugs can seem to be everywhere.
  • It has been revealed that only 8.5% of eligible adults in the study filled a prescription for either drug within six months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study of more than half a million privately insured adults found that where patients received care was linked to whether they filled a prescription for weight-loss drugs.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold as Wegovy and Zepbound, and the two weight-loss drugs can seem to be everywhere.

It has been revealed that only 8.5% of eligible adults in the study filled a prescription for either drug within six months. Patients were more likely to fill one if they received care in areas where more residents had a college degree.

This gap grew as the drugs became more common.

Recent findings suggest that private insurance was held by every one of these patients. Coverage alone was therefore not enough to make access equal.

The study was led by Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst at Boston University School of Public Health.

He was based in the school’s Department of Global Health. Le worked with Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at the school.

Insurance billing records were used for the analysis. Such records can show a pattern in who received a prescription. The cause of that pattern cannot be shown by them.

Stokes stated insurers pay for these drugs far more readily when a patient has diabetes.

He called people with overweight or obesity “a population that has been left behind.”.

Sources indicate that the records were drawn from a national database of insurance claims. More than 175 million people are covered by that database.

From it, Le and Stokes selected adults between the ages of 18 and 64. They first met the study’s eligibility criteria between July 2021 and June 2025.

Industry observers note that clinical guidelines decide who qualifies for the drugs. The bar is a body mass index, or BMI, of at least 30. A BMI of at least 27 is also accepted alongside a weight-related condition.

High blood pressure and sleep apnea are two examples.

Recent findings suggest that people with type 2 diabetes were excluded from the study. People on Medicare or Medicaid were left out as well, along with those without insurance. That left 512,389 patients.

The researchers checked whether patients filled a prescription for semaglutide or tirzepatide within six months of first meeting the study’s eligibility criteria.

Ozempic and Wegovy are the brand names of semaglutide. Tirzepatide goes by Mounjaro and Zepbound.

It has been revealed that versions labeled for diabetes are at times prescribed for obesity. These prescriptions were included in the count.

Industry observers note that the clinics were compared through the ZIP code of each patient’s health care provider. Each ZIP code was looked up in the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey.

The survey reports how many residents hold a bachelor’s degree or higher. On that basis, patients were split into four equal groups.

In a recent development, among patients diagnosed in the summer of 2021, 1.9% were prescribed one of the two drugs within six months. For patients diagnosed in the spring of 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%.

Even then, about five of every six eligible patients had no prescription after six months.

Semaglutide was approved for weight management by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in June 2021. Tirzepatide got the same approval in November 2023.

Both belong to a class called GLP-1 drugs. In clinical trials, drugs in this class have helped people lose weight. They have also protected the heart.

In a recent development, both drugs were in short supply at times during the study. When semaglutide was scarce, tirzepatide prescriptions rose quickly. The reverse was seen when tirzepatide was scarce.

Recent findings suggest that le and Stokes took that as a sign that doctors swap one drug for the other. By the second half of 2024, tirzepatide had become the more prescribed of the two.

Recent findings suggest that at first, prescription rates were about the same in all four neighborhood groups. The rates began to differ in late 2022.

Recent findings suggest that by spring 2025, 21.7% of patients seen in areas with the highest share of college graduates filled a prescription. In the other three groups, the share ranged from 14.4% to 15.2%.

The results were then adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI and other illnesses. The number of doctor visits was taken into account as well.

Between 2021 and 2023, odds of a prescription were 15% lower in the least educated group. The most educated group served as the benchmark. For 2024 and 2025, that figure reached 35%.

Among men, the neighborhood gap was wider than among women. The overweight range indicated the widest gap of any BMI category. Odds in the least educated group were 40% lower there.

For the most severe obesity category, the difference shrank to 10%.

Recent findings suggest that le and Stokes offered a possible reason. More illnesses tend to be on record for patients with severe obesity. An insurer’s approval rules may be easier for them to meet.

According to recent reports, by the spring of 2025, 20.7% of women were prescribed one of the drugs. Among men, the figure was 11.9%. After the same adjustments, men had less than half the odds that women had.

Age was linked to prescriptions too. Adults ages 35 to 54 had about twice the odds of adults ages 18 to 24.

Black patients and Hispanic patients each had 11% lower odds than white patients. About a third of the records had no race or ethnicity listed, though. Those two estimates may be shakier as a result.

It has been revealed that as BMI rose, so did prescriptions. Even so, most patients in the most severe obesity category went without one. Only about one in five of those diagnosed in the spring of 2025 got a prescription.

Earlier research suggests that early treatment can prevent or ease later complications, Le and Stokes wrote.

Among patients who first qualified in summer 2021, 1.9% filled a prescription for either drug within six months.

Recent findings suggest that by spring 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%. Even then, about five in six eligible patients had no recorded fill within six months.

Industry observers note that the forms for that approval are filled in by the staff of the clinic. Fewer of those forms may be handled by a clinic where staff are few.

Recent findings suggest that cost was named second. Different amounts are charged to patients by different employer health prepares for the same drug.

In a 2026 study, 8,914 privately insured adults who had started semaglutide were followed by other researchers.

After accounting for other factors, researchers found that patients who paid more than $168 per 30-day supply were 9 percentage points more likely to fall short of the study’s refill target than those who paid $21 or less.

Recent findings suggest that A review of approval rules and of patient costs was requested by Le. He also asked for help with approval forms for clinics that are short of staff.

Payment programs that reward clinics for quality targets were mentioned in the paper as well. If prescribing rates were made a target, a short-staffed clinic could be penalized for the shortage, not its care.

The ZIP code of the clinic was held by Le and Stokes for each of the 512,389 patients.

It has been revealed that the income and the schooling of each patient were not held by them. The study therefore cannot assign the gap to the clinics or to the patients.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold to some people by direct-to-consumer sellers and no insurer is involved.

Sales of that kind are not recorded in claims and were not counted by the researchers. Which groups of patients buy the drugs in this way is not known.

A diagnosis had already been given by a doctor to every patient in the study.

Diagnosis codes are applied unevenly and milder obesity is often left unrecorded, Le and Stokes wrote. Some adults who were eligible may have been missed for that reason.

Industry observers note that more than 60 data sources are combined in the database that was used. It was still not described by the authors as a match for all insured Americans.

Industry observers note that the cause of the neighborhood gap has not been found. Insurance rules, prescribing habits and patients’ awareness of the drugs were listed by the authors for future studies.

Records of direct-to-consumer sales were also suggested by them, to show who is missing from the claims.

The full study was published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, upcoming prescription data suggest.

Sources indicate that monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the upcoming study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

In a recent development, the latest study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

It has been revealed that “Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” indicates Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

In a recent development, there are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The newly introduced study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.
