High school and college teams can win up to $20,000 each by designing technology for NASA’s Moon Base, and sign-ups close January 25

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that NASA's Moon Base Challenge invites U.S.
  • The Moon Base Challenge was declared on November 8 at a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida.
  • Teams do not need prior specialized engineering or technical experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that NASA's Moon Base Challenge invites U.S. high school and college teams to design technology for a lunar base.

The Moon Base Challenge was declared on November 8 at a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. It is open to student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools.

Teams do not need prior specialized engineering or technical experience. In the final round, they can explain an idea with a mock-up made of cardboard. Students have helped with real research before, as when students helped astronomers track a rare alien comet.

NASA is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work and explore in the lunar South Pole region. The agency indicates a permanent human presence on the Moon paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars.

Industry observers note that the region may contain resources that could one day help support explorers. NASA looks to send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE to search for evidence of water ice and other resources there.

Industry observers note that “We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute.”.

“Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for,” remarked Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program.

Each team picks one of six categories: power generation and storage, habitat construction using lunar materials, life-support systems, surface mobility, communication networks, or astronaut safety.

Habitat ideas can go beyond engineering, since researchers have argued that Moon bases could be designed to ease anxiety and homesickness.

It has been revealed that the designs have to work in a harsh place. According to the official rules, they must handle vacuum, radiation, micrometeorites, abrasive dust and temperature swings from 248 degrees Fahrenheit (120 degrees Celsius) to minus 274 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 170 degrees Celsius).

They also have to cope with day and night cycles that last two weeks each, and rely as little as possible on supplies from Earth.

Water is one of the hard parts: one analysis found that the Moon can generate enough power for a permanent city, but not enough water.

A team has two to five students and an adult coach, at least 18, who holds a formal role at the team’s school or organization, such as a teacher, faculty member or club advisor.

There are three divisions, judged separately. High school teams are for students in grades 9 to 12 who were between 13 and 18 years old when registration opened, including home-schooled students.

The other two divisions are for undergraduates at two-year schools, such as community and technical colleges, and at four-year colleges and universities.

Industry observers note that those students must be at least 16. A mixed team competes in the division of its most advanced or oldest member. Middle school and graduate students cannot take part.

Students must be U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents or foreign nationals who are full-time students at an eligible U.S. school and physically live in the United States for the whole challenge.

Every student has to create an account on NASA’s STEM Gateway, and only the student team lead submits the application. Coaches should not register there; they are linked to the team later on the organizer’s platform.

In the first phase, teams write a Concept Overview Paper of 5 to 7 pages. It must explain how the idea works and how it survives lunar conditions, and include at least one page of diagrams or other visuals. Papers are due February 22, 2027.

Up to 100 teams will be named finalists on March 11. They will then record a pitch video of up to 10 minutes, with a deck of up to 15 slides, due April 19.

Recent findings suggest that finalists can explain their design with hand-drawn diagrams, posterboard schematics or low-cost mock-ups made of cardboard, foam or household materials. CAD software and physical prototypes are allowed but optional. Winners will be confirmed on May 6, 2027.

NASA’s announcement calls it a $1 million challenge, and the challenge website says up to $1 million in monetary awards are available.

The official rules for the 2026-27 challenge, however, list a total maximum prize payout of $500,000, and neither source explains the difference.

Sources indicate that each of up to 100 finalist teams gets $1,400. In the final phase, up to 12 grand prize winners get $20,000 each, and up to 12 runners-up get $10,000 each.

The rules also say payments depend on federal funding and NASA’s final approval, and NASA does not have to award the full amount if too few entries meet its quality bar.

The money goes to a U.S. bank account designated by the team’s coach, who decides how it is shared. Teams keep the rights to what they invent, although NASA may negotiate a license to use it.

A virtual opening symposium introducing the categories is set for December 3. Registered teams can also join live question-and-answer webinars on January 14 and February 11, 2027. The organizers say all dates may change.

Industry observers note that the challenge is run for NASA by the Institute of Competition Sciences. Full rules and registration steps are on the official challenge website.

The information was obtained from NASA’s announcement, its Moon Base page and the official rules.

At the Races: Regional realignment

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • Recent findings suggest that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Latest England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

Recent findings suggest that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged Fresh England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

In a recent development, three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

It has been revealed that tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

In a recent development, redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a newly introduced congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Industry observers note that run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

According to recent reports, tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

In a recent development, guv patch: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Sources indicate that senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have released a fresh organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, latest members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

Industry observers note that ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Upcoming York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

In a recent development, here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

According to recent reports, how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Upcoming York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Newly introduced York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

Recent findings suggest that if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#100526. Traces of insecticide in cord blood raise upcoming questions about childhood development

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1214 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Traces of insecticide in cord blood raise upcoming questions about childhood development

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Japanese study linked insecticide exposure before a child's birth to lower scores on certain thinking tests at age nine.
  • Two compounds linked to widely used insecticides turned up in umbilical cord blood in a Japanese study.
  • At age 9, children with higher levels of one compound at birth scored lower on a test of processing speed, while those with higher levels of the other scored lower on a test of visual reasoning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Japanese study linked insecticide exposure before a child's birth to lower scores on certain thinking tests at age nine.

Two compounds linked to widely used insecticides turned up in umbilical cord blood in a Japanese study.

At age 9, children with higher levels of one compound at birth scored lower on a test of processing speed, while those with higher levels of the other scored lower on a test of visual reasoning.

Earlier tests, given between 10 and 32 months, yielded no clear links after researchers accounted for the number of comparisons they made.

The researchers wrote that any association may hinge on the age of the child and the skill examined. Just 200 children took part. Proof that the insecticides caused the weaker scores cannot be drawn from this work.

Sources indicate that abir Nagata and Kenji Tsuchiya, a professor, headed the investigation. Both are based at the Research Center for Child Mental Development at Hamamatsu University School of Medicine.

They are also affiliated with a graduate school run jointly by The University of Osaka and four other Japanese universities.

It has been revealed that the growth of a child’s brain and abilities is referred to by scientists as neurodevelopment. Children in earlier work on these insecticides were seldom followed beyond early childhood.

“Previous studies have largely focused on neurodevelopmental outcomes at a single time point,” Nagata stated.

Industry observers note that nicotine served as the chemical model for neonicotinoids. Their target is a receptor on nerve cells that normally binds one of the body’s chemical messengers.

Insects carry these receptors and so do humans. Within a fetus, the authors wrote, the receptors assist nerve cells in maturing and connecting.

According to recent reports, harm to bees is what the insecticides are chiefly known for. Over a quarter of global insecticide sales are now attributed to them.

According to recent reports, food and drinking water have both been found to contain residues. Nationwide monitoring in Japan has picked up neonicotinoids in tap water throughout the year.

Animal experiments have been cited as grounds for concern. Altered brain structure followed exposure during brain development in those experiments. Impaired movement, learning and attention were documented as well.

Recent findings suggest that links with early development have been reported in several studies of children. Agreement between those studies has been poor, however.

All of the children are enrolled in the Hamamatsu Birth Cohort, an ongoing project on child development. The project recruited 1,258 babies. Their births took place in Hamamatsu, Japan, between December 2007 and March 2012.

Sources indicate that urine from pregnant women was the usual source of insecticide measurements in earlier research. What actually reached the baby in the womb is not shown directly by urine. Umbilical cord blood drawn at birth offers a direct measure.

Limited resources meant that cord blood from only 200 randomly selected children could be analyzed. Serum, the liquid fraction of blood, was screened by a laboratory for insecticides and their breakdown products.

Of the ten compounds measured, just two turned up often. Dinotefuran was detected in 104 of the 200 samples, or 52%.

A breakdown product of acetamiprid, a second insecticide, was the other. Its detection rate was 62.5%, or 125 samples.

In a recent development, the team split the children into low, middle and high groups for each of the two chemicals. Detection was seldom possible in the low group, which was used as the comparison.

Industry observers note that quantities were minute. A typical reading in the high dinotefuran group was 0.07 billionths of a gram per milliliter of serum.

Sources indicate that the researchers scheduled five rounds of testing between 10 and 32 months of age. Depending on the visit, 185 to 195 children had enough data to be included in the analysis.

Toddlers with higher levels scored below the low group in a handful of comparisons. Large body movements at 10 and 14 months were weaker in the middle dinotefuran group.

The reverse was seen once. Hand and finger skills at 18 months were stronger in the middle group for the acetamiprid breakdown product.

It has been revealed that the team ran 50 comparisons per chemical over the toddler period. Some results will appear meaningful purely by chance when that many comparisons are run.

According to recent reports, statistical significance was lost for every toddler result after the researchers corrected for this. Across ages and skills, no consistent pattern emerged.

A standard four-part intelligence test was completed by 178 of the 200 children at age 9. Differences on two of the four parts survived the same correction.

Processing speed was lower among children in the middle dinotefuran group. The measure captures how fast a child gets through simple tasks.

It has been revealed that the shortfall against the low group came to roughly 7 points. An average score on this test is 100.

According to recent reports, perceptual reasoning was weaker in the high group for the acetamiprid breakdown product. Visual puzzles and pattern spotting are what this part of the test relies on. The gap on this part was almost as wide.

Overall IQ scores were lower in those same two groups as well.

Rising insecticide levels did not bring a steady decline in scores. Processing speed was also lower in the high dinotefuran group. That difference was smaller, though, and chance could account for it.

In a recent development, tsuchiya stated the contrast with the toddler findings may reflect links specific to certain skills and ages. On that reading, no single lasting pattern runs through childhood.

The children were only observed as they grew up, and nothing about their exposure was controlled. A link can therefore be identified by the study, whereas a cause cannot be proven.

A single blood sample taken at delivery supplied each child’s insecticide level. The timing of exposure during pregnancy cannot be learned from one sample. Neither can the degree to which exposure varied.

Adjustments were made for each child’s sex and age, premature birth and the education of both parents.

Diet went unmeasured, as did lead, other heavy metals and the parents’ own thinking skills. Part of the gap in scores might be explained by such factors.

Dinotefuran levels at birth were also higher in children who took the age 9 test than in the rest. The results could be skewed by that difference.

Too few samples contained the eight other compounds for them to be analyzed, alone or combined.

Only 178 children contributed to the age 9 results. The authors wrote that estimates from a sample of this size are imprecise. Weaker links may also have gone undetected.

Whether other groups of children show the same links is the next question. Why the links would surface at age 9 and not sooner also remains unexplained.

Sources indicate that the authors called for larger studies. Exposure would need to be measured several times during pregnancy in such studies. Testing of the children would continue through middle childhood.

For now, a single group of children in one Japanese city is the source of the evidence.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#100525. Industry News: Glaciers lose ice faster where they meet lakes, but there’s more to the story

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1474 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Glaciers lose ice faster where they meet lakes, but there’s more to the story

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Glaciers that end in lakes lost ice about 65% faster than those that end on land, but climate and terrain explained more of the variation than lakes did.
  • Meltwater is often collected in the hollow that a retreating glacier leaves behind.
  • Sources indicate that once such a lake has formed, the neighboring ice can be lost more quickly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glaciers that end in lakes lost ice about 65% faster than those that end on land, but climate and terrain explained more of the variation than lakes did.

Meltwater is often collected in the hollow that a retreating glacier leaves behind.

Sources indicate that once such a lake has formed, the neighboring ice can be lost more quickly. The lake melts the glacier front below the waterline, and pieces break off more easily.

According to recent reports, the size of that effect has now been estimated across the world’s glaciers by an international team. Between 2000 and 2020, glaciers ending in lakes were found to lose ice about 65% faster than those on land.

It has been revealed that in the researchers’ model, lake characteristics accounted for about 11% of the differences in ice loss the model could explain. Climate and glacier terrain accounted for most of the rest.

It has been revealed that the work was led by Shaochun Zhao and Guoqing Zhang. Both are at the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Their 15 co-authors work in China, Europe, and the United States. One of them is Tobias Bolch of the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology.

In a recent development, the team worked from satellite images and a statistical model. No instruments were placed at the ice.

Glacial lakes were mapped everywhere outside Antarctica using images from the Landsat satellites. The images were taken around 2000 and again around 2020.

Recent findings suggest that software trained to recognize lakes drew the first outlines. Those outlines were then checked and corrected by eye.

A lake had to cover about two-thirds of an acre (0.0027 square kilometers) to count.

Industry observers note that glacial lakes of every kind increased 9% in number, to 160,332. Lakes touching a glacier increased 35%, a gain of 3,567 lakes.

Three-quarters of the water added to glacial lakes went into lakes touching ice.

According to recent reports, the team estimated that lakes in direct contact with glaciers held about 16 cubic miles (66 cubic kilometers) more water by 2020. Volume was worked out from surface area with the help of depth surveys of 299 lakes.

Bolch’s university put that volume in city terms. Poured over Vienna in an even layer, the water would stand about 525 feet (160 meters) deep.

Worldwide growth of glacial lakes since 1990 had already been documented in the same journal by a 2020 survey.

According to recent reports, in that survey, however, lakes were not sorted according to whether they touch ice. That detail was required for the present study.

Industry observers note that expansion of ice-touching lakes by more than 39 square miles (100 square kilometers) was recorded in only two regions. These were Alaska and the southern Andes. Fifteen of the 20 lakes with the largest growth are located in these two regions.

The largest single gain, roughly 20 square miles (53 square kilometers), was measured at a lake in Alaska. Within the southern Andes, growth was concentrated around the two Patagonian ice fields.

Most of the growth came from a small number of large lakes. Although 2,946 lakes expanded in total, 810 of them grew by more than 25 acres (0.1 square kilometers).

Those 810 lakes accounted for 92% of the total area gain.

A further 4,538 ice-touching lakes were formed between 2000 and 2020.

Contact with the ice was not maintained everywhere. During the same period, 1,645 lakes became detached from their glaciers. In Upcoming Zealand, eight lakes were detached while only three new ones were formed.

In a recent development, to compare glaciers, the team relied on the Randolph Glacier Inventory, a global catalog of glacier outlines. It was combined with an existing record of glacier ice loss.

Of roughly 214,000 glaciers, 7,121 terminate in a lake and 1,512 in the sea, while the remainder end on land.

Sources indicate that ice loss is expressed by glaciologists as a depth of water. This is the depth the lost ice would produce if spread across the whole glacier.

By that measure, lake-ending glaciers lost about 26 inches (0.66 meters) a year.

For land-ending glaciers the figure was about 16 inches (0.40 meters), and for sea-ending glaciers about 14 inches (0.36 meters).

Bolch was part of a team that found a similar gap among Himalayan glaciers in 2019.

It has been revealed that the fastest ice loss was not seen at these glaciers everywhere. In Iceland, Svalbard, the Russian Arctic, and northern Arctic Canada, they lost less ice than land-ending ones.

Industry observers note that A possible reason was suggested by the authors. Lake-ending glaciers in those regions are considerably larger and lie at higher elevations.

In a recent development, over those 20 years, about 1.5 trillion tons (1,362 billion metric tons) were lost by lake-ending glaciers. This amounts to roughly 28% of all glacier ice lost worldwide.

Recent findings suggest that studies of single glaciers had disagreed about how much a lake matters. At two glaciers in southeastern Tibet, the loss was dominated at certain stages by ice breaking off into a lake.

Studies in the western Himalaya and British Columbia suggested that lakes played a secondary role.

Industry observers note that to weigh the causes, machine learning was used. Here, a program learns which measurements best predict an outcome. Three such programs analyzed the lake-ending glaciers.

According to recent reports, for each glacier, the lake’s size and growth were recorded together with 20 years of temperature and precipitation data. Slope, elevation, and latitude were also included.

It has been revealed that of the ice loss the best program could explain, 46% was attributed to a glacier’s shape and position. Climate was assigned 43% and lakes 11%.

Each share carries an uncertainty of 7 to 10 percentage points.

Steeper and higher glaciers tended to lose less ice. Glaciers whose lakes grew more tended to lose more.

In a recent development, the lakes’ share was highest in regions where lakes had expanded substantially. It was about 14% to 15% in Scandinavia, Alaska, and the southern Andes, and 5% in northern Arctic Canada.

Bolch ranked the causes the same way, placing climate and terrain ahead of lakes, which “significantly exacerbate” the loss.

Recent findings suggest that deeper lake water pushes up harder on the front of a glacier, which helps floating ice detach. Lake water also melts ice below the surface.

Recent findings suggest that A glacier’s loss is measured by satellites that track the height of its surface. Ice lost underwater can’t be seen that way.

In a recent development, that uncounted loss was estimated at about 62 billion tons (56 billion metric tons) for 2000 to 2020. If it were counted, the total for lake-ending glaciers would be raised by roughly 4%.

With other volume estimates, that figure reaches as much as 8%.

In a recent development, water that would otherwise reach the ocean is also held back by lakes. Between 2000 and 2023, melting glaciers added about 0.7 inches (18 millimeters) to global sea level.

It has been revealed that by comparison, only a small amount was stored in glacial lakes from 2000 to 2020. The team calculated it as about one hundredth of an inch (0.24 millimeters) of sea level. That estimate assumes all the water in the lakes came from glaciers.

The results should make forecasts of glacier change more accurate, Bolch remarked.

Mountain regions and the lowlands below them have the most use for such forecasts, Bolch added. A significant share of their water comes from meltwater.

The best program accounted for a little more than half of the differences in ice loss among glaciers. Several of its lake measurements were stand-ins.

Depth matters most right where water meets ice, and direct measurements there are scarce. The team therefore relied on an average depth, which was estimated from each lake’s surface area.

The length of ice touching water came from a single date. The warmth of each lake could only be approximated, using air temperature and lake volume.

Sources indicate that ice thickness at the glacier front wasn’t in the analysis, the authors wrote. Neither was the shape of the ground beneath it.

Anyone assessing the danger of outburst floods from glacial lakes can use the findings too, Bolch said.

Industry observers note that future research could measure water depth and temperature at glacier fronts. How the line where ice meets water shifts over time could also be tracked.

Physical models built for lake-ending glaciers would give a more accurate answer than statistics, the authors wrote. Such models already exist for glaciers that end in the sea.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Climate Change.

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is key for talking, too.

Sources indicate that data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, states neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

Recent findings suggest that A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, stated in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The newly introduced research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, claims neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Industry observers note that scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” noted UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

It has been revealed that some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang stated.

Physicists have found half the answer to why some materials carry electricity with no loss

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In one copper oxide, flickering electron spins drive high-temperature superconductors, and coupling strength sets where resistance ends.
  • Every wire wastes a little of the electricity that runs through it, which is why a phone charger gets warm.
  • A family of copper-oxide ceramics become superconductors at temperatures well above the rest, and physicists have argued for decades about why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In one copper oxide, flickering electron spins drive high-temperature superconductors, and coupling strength sets where resistance ends.

Every wire wastes a little of the electricity that runs through it, which is why a phone charger gets warm. Cool certain materials far enough and that waste disappears.

A family of copper-oxide ceramics become superconductors at temperatures well above the rest, and physicists have argued for decades about why.

For one branch of that family, a team has now matched the strength of one interaction to the temperature at which the loss vanishes.

Electrons in these materials scatter off rapid flickers in the magnetism of the surrounding atoms. The stronger that scattering, the higher the temperature at which the material stops wasting energy.

So, the authors concluded, those magnetic flickers are what pair the electrons up.

That covers only half of the superconductor family, and the half with the highest temperatures behaves differently. So the answer isn’t complete, and the authors remarked so.

Industry observers note that nigel Hussey, a professor of physics at the University of Bristol who also holds a post at Radboud University in the Netherlands, co-led the work. Caitlin Duffy, now a postdoctoral researcher at the French research agency CNRS, ran the experiments.

“Through measurements carried out at the European Magnetic Field Laboratory in the Netherlands and subsequent careful analysis, we have found the smoking gun which solves part of the equation and explains what causes this perplexing state,” Hussey said.

In a normal metal, electrons bump into vibrating atoms as they travel, and each collision wastes a little energy as heat. In the oldest known superconductors, those same vibrations do something else at very low temperatures.

They nudge electrons into pairs, and paired electrons flow without resistance.

It has been revealed that that theory has a useful feature. The strength of the pull between vibrations and electrons reveals up in a metal’s resistance above the transition, and the same strength sets the transition temperature. Measure one and you can predict the other.

According to recent reports, the copper-oxide materials become superconductors at much higher temperatures, too high for vibrating atoms to explain. Physicists call that temperature Tc.

The leading candidate for a replacement glue has long been the electrons’ own spins, which act like tiny magnets and flicker in step with their neighbors.

What was missing was a measurement tying the strength of that flickering to Tc, the way resistance ties vibrations to it in ordinary metals.

Collaborators at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing grew a thin film of lanthanum cerium copper oxide, one atomic layer at a time.

Along the film, the cerium content changed smoothly from one end to the other. Cerium adds electrons to the material, and the amount sets Tc.

At one end, the film became superconducting at about 25 kelvin, or roughly -415°F (-248°C), which is close to the best this material can do.

Recent findings suggest that at the other end it never did. Between those ends sat 19 distinct compositions, measured across two films grown the same way, so the amount of disorder stayed the same from end to end.

The team patterned electrical contacts along the film and measured its resistance at each position while varying the temperature and the magnetic field.

The field came from a 35-tesla magnet at the High Field Magnet Laboratory in Nijmegen. This is far stronger than the magnet inside a hospital MRI scanner.

In a recent development, A magnetic field bends the paths of electrons. How much the resistance rises in a field depends on how often the electrons scatter and from where.

In these films, the pattern pointed to scattering concentrated at particular spots, and those spots matched the ones where electrons meet the flickering spins of neighboring atoms.

According to recent reports, the team then fit the resistance and the field response at all 13 measured positions on one film. Only one number was allowed to change from position to position – the strength of that scattering.

Across the film, as Tc fell from 25 kelvin to zero, that number fell tenfold. Duffy said the field measurements were what made the identification possible.

“Employing some analytical tricks on the data obtained in high magnetic fields, we were then able to identify the dominant source of resistance in this material as scattering off the fluctuating spins,” stated Duffy.

“The correlation between the strength of this interaction and Tc then confirmed that the origin for superconductivity in this material is indeed the interaction between the conduction electrons and spin fluctuations,” she added.

One consequence cuts against an earlier idea. Some physicists had argued that the resistance in these superconductors sits at a universal quantum limit.

The scattering strength here varied by a factor of ten across the film, so in this branch of the family, at least, it does not.

Sources indicate that copper-oxide superconductors come in two kinds. Adding electrons, as cerium does here, makes one kind. Removing electrons, which physicists call adding holes, makes the other. The hole-doped materials reach the highest transition temperatures of all.

According to recent reports, A tempting guess is that hole-doped materials simply couple more strongly to the same magnetic flickers. However, the team’s earlier high-field measurements on those materials say otherwise.

In the state physicists call a strange metal, their resistance responds to a magnetic field in a way the same model can’t reproduce. No standard picture of electrons as individual particles has yet accounted for it.

“Although electron- and hole-doped cuprates are made from the same cloth, they are stitched together in different patterns,” Hussey explained.

It has been revealed that the result rests on one material, measured on two films, and on a model in which electrons still behave as particles with definite paths. The model’s success here is itself evidence, the authors wrote, because the same approach fails on the hole-doped side.

“While we have found the first key ingredient, the task now is to go and find the second,” Hussey said.

It has been revealed that what the second ingredient is, nobody has measured. Finding it, the authors wrote, may take an approach that goes beyond the standard theory of superconductivity, or beyond treating electrons as individual particles at all.

The hole-doped materials are where that search has to happen.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Physics.

Latest Update: Researchers find a clever way to use everyday garbage to make greener cement instead of burning fossil fuels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review of 211 studies finds refuse-derived fuel could replace coal in cement kilns, but fuel standards and rules still don't line up.
  • Industry observers note that plastic bags, blended fabrics, and treated wood are hard to recycle, and a lot of waste like that goes to landfill.
  • Industry observers note that feeding kilns with processed trash instead of coal could ease both problems at once.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review of 211 studies finds refuse-derived fuel could replace coal in cement kilns, but fuel standards and rules still don't line up.

Industry observers note that plastic bags, blended fabrics, and treated wood are hard to recycle, and a lot of waste like that goes to landfill. Cement kilns, meanwhile, burn coal for the heat that turns limestone into cement, a product behind an estimated 8 percent of the carbon dioxide people put into the air each year.

Industry observers note that feeding kilns with processed trash instead of coal could ease both problems at once. A review of 35 years of research finds the idea gaining ground while the basics stay unsettled.

Geethmi Thisakya, a Ph.D. candidate in the School of Civil Engineering and Construction Management at Adelaide University, led the review with her supervisors Navodana Rodrigo, Chamitha Wijewickrama, and George Zillante.

Recent findings suggest that her subject is refuse-derived fuel. It’s waste processed into something with more heat per pound, less moisture, and more even particles than raw trash. Burning it alongside coal in a kiln is known as co-processing.

“Previous research has highlighted the potential of refuse-derived fuel to turn suitable waste materials into a useful resource rather than sending them to landfill,” Thisakya mentioned.

Sources indicate that the team searched the Web of Science database for every study on refuse-derived fuel in cement making between 1991 and July 2025, and found 211 in English. Almost all of that interest is recent.

The earliest paper that fit dates from 1992, and output stayed low until a rise after 2013.

According to recent reports, more than 80 percent of the papers were published in the past 11 years, with a peak of 24 in 2023 alone. Forty-eight records, including seven regulatory documents, were read in full.

China produced the most studies, 29 of them, followed by Germany with 21, Poland with 19, and Brazil with 12. Africa and Latin America barely appear, even though the team sees them as places where the fuel could catch on.

The confusion starts with vocabulary. Refuse-derived fuel has a stricter cousin, solid recovered fuel, which has to meet an international standard called ISO 21640.

That standard sorts the fuel into five classes by how much heat it gives off and how much chlorine and mercury it contains.

Refuse-derived fuel typically has no such standard, yet studies and regulations use the two names interchangeably, the review found.

It has been revealed that some papers call the ISO classes “RDF classes” when the standard defines them for solid recovered fuel, and fuel that meets the standard is sometimes labeled refuse-derived fuel anyway. Sometimes that’s deliberate shorthand, since the standardized fuel is a refined subset of the broader one.

For a kiln operator, the muddle isn’t academic. It affects which fuel a plant will accept, what the emissions paperwork says, and what a supply contract means.

“However, our review reveals that realizing this potential requires more than simply replacing coal with waste. We need consistent fuel quality, clear regulations and stronger evidence about the environmental and economic impacts,” Thisakya noted.

The European Union has the most developed rulebook. Its rules set emission limits for kilns that burn waste fuel, assign the codes that let the fuel cross borders, and ban high-energy waste from landfill.

One rule pulls the other way, however. As Europe pushes plastics recycling harder, the mixed plastics that make up much of the fuel will get scarcer.

According to recent reports, elsewhere the picture is patchy. In the United States the fuel falls under the Clean Air Act and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, which governs waste handling.

According to recent reports, germany separates the two fuel types in law. Poland still classifies refuse-derived fuel as waste, so moving and storing it needs a waste license. Indonesia pays a feed-in tariff to encourage it.

Peer-reviewed work rarely compares how these regimes affect uptake in cement plants, the review found.

Regulators rank what to do with trash in a hierarchy: prevention first, then reuse, then recycling, then “other recovery,” then disposal.

The authors place refuse-derived fuel in that fourth tier, and in the “recover” slot of the circular-economy list that runs from refuse to recover.

It has been revealed that recycling should still come first, the authors wrote. Refuse-derived fuel is a route for the burnable leftovers that landfills would otherwise take. Other routes to cleaner cement, from different rocks to kilns that capture carbon, fall outside the review.

The search covered one database and one language, so studies indexed elsewhere or written in other languages were missed.

The authors wrote that regional work from non-English-speaking countries is the likeliest gap. They also excluded power plants and district heating, which burn the same fuel, so lessons from those sectors didn’t carry over.

Nor does the review settle how much carbon the switch saves. Early life-cycle studies have weighed the trade-offs of replacing coal, but the authors found none built around the specific conditions of a cement kiln.

That analysis is on their research agenda, along with tests of how the fuel performs in different regions and plants.

What the review asks for next is that number, measured for a cement kiln, before the construction sector counts the switch as a saving.

The full study was published in the journal International Journal of Building Pathology and Adaptation.

Industry News: Parasite outbreaks in the food supply chain highlight how much public attention hurts bagged salad sales

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google searches for "cyclospora" predicted where bagged salad sales fell during parasite outbreaks.
  • A food recall looks like a supply problem: bags pulled from the shelf, a gap in the produce case.
  • Weekly purchases ran 3.89 percent below normal, on average, across those outbreak and recall periods, and the missing sales added up to roughly $374 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google searches for "cyclospora" predicted where bagged salad sales fell during parasite outbreaks.

A food recall looks like a supply problem: bags pulled from the shelf, a gap in the produce case. During six cyclospora outbreaks between 2018 and 2022, stores revealed no sign of cutting back on bagged salad, and prices barely moved, yet households bought less of it anyway.

Weekly purchases ran 3.89 percent below normal, on average, across those outbreak and recall periods, and the missing sales added up to roughly $374 million.

Where sales fell depended not only on where people got sick but on where people were typing “cyclospora” into Google.

It has been revealed that xuerui Yang ran the analysis as a doctoral student at The Ohio State University. She is now a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Florida’s Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS).

The dollar figure is an estimate from household purchase records, and the search counts stand in for a region’s exposure to cyclospora outbreak news, not for what any one shopper read.

It has been revealed that in an interview with Earth.com, Yang put the main lesson in one line. “News travels through media markets, not state lines,” she mentioned.

In a recent development, cyclospora cayetanensis, a single-celled parasite first identified in 1993, can live in soil or water for months. It survives the chlorine washes that processing plants run produce through.

Like other kinds of food poisoning, the infection usually brings watery diarrhea, cramps, bloating and a lost appetite, and most people recover on their own.

People with weakened immune systems can become severely ill or stay sick for a long time.

Industry observers note that large cyclospora outbreaks were rare before 2018. That year, reported outbreaks were tied to 1,165 illnesses nationwide, and the numbers have stayed high since. Packaged salads have been implicated more and more often.

Yang’s team picked six large multistate outbreaks from 2018 to 2022. Four of them traced to bagged salad mix. Together, they accounted for 2,157 illnesses, about two-thirds of every outbreak-linked case reported to the CDC in that span. The rest were smaller events.

Recent findings suggest that recalls followed the 2018, 2019 and 2020 outbreaks. The 2018 and 2020 salad recalls were traced to a single U.S. manufacturer and spread to store brands. The last two outbreaks in the study ended with no recall at all.

Earlier research on food scares measured public attention through news coverage, which is usually counted by state or for the whole country.

Yang’s team used something finer: how often people searched Google for “cyclospora,” week by week, in each of 210 media markets.

Nielsen draws those markets to map which TV and radio stations a household receives, and they follow broadcast signals rather than borders, so one market can straddle two states.

A second index, built from the public Google Trends tool, tracked general searches for salad, lettuce and basil, with outbreak terms filtered out.

The team matched both against weekly purchase records from a NielsenIQ panel of about 46,000 households a year, 12 million household-weeks in all.

The search index behaved the way a news measure should. Spikes in “cyclospora” searches lined up with spikes in news coverage.

During the 2020 cyclospora outbreak, search activity broadly followed where illnesses were being reported, and Illinois and Iowa reported the most.

Searches for “cyclospora” were linked to the steepest declines in purchases, and general searches about salad and leafy greens were linked to much smaller ones.

It has been revealed that the authors read that as information working in two directions. News that names the parasite raises alarm, while ordinary searching about salad tends to settle it.

Recalls mattered on their own. A single week of a cyclospora recall cut purchases in affected states by about 3.2 percent compared with ordinary weeks, and recall periods ran 22 to 31 weeks.

In a recent development, households whose salad purchases included one recalled brand bought no less than usual, but households whose purchases included two or more recalled brands bought noticeably less. One recalled brand, it seems, made little difference; a second one did.

“What people read online shows up in what they put in their carts,” Yang said.

To check that worry rather than empty shelves explained the decline, the team pulled store-level sales records for 2018 and 2020, the two years with salad recalls.

Store by store, across more than 100 million transactions, there was no sign that retailers cut what they stocked, and prices barely moved.

It has been revealed that media markets gave the team a natural test. In the authors’ example, someone in Washington, D.C., watches the same local news as someone in Virginia.

So a Virginia cyclospora outbreak reaches D.C. households even when no contaminated salad was ever sold there.

Industry observers note that in states with no reported illness, households that shared a media market with an affected state bought 3.33 percent less salad per week than in outbreak-free weeks. Those households were a small slice of the data, so the estimate is less precise than the main one.

Yang doesn’t read that as a case for softer warnings. “People in unaffected states still bought less salad when they shared local news with an affected state,” she told Earth.com.

Sources indicate that “And we don’t see this as a reason for quieter warnings. When shoppers stayed away from affected products, they’re also protecting themselves. What matters is clear, timely information.”.

It has been revealed that the 2020 outbreak was the biggest in the study, with 771 illnesses across 14 states. Counting the recall that followed, it reached 33 states and more than 190 million people, and it produced the largest loss, close to $190 million.

The bigger outbreak, though, drew the smaller reaction from shoppers.

Recent findings suggest that purchases fell about 3.1 percent in 2020 against 4.6 percent two years earlier. Furthermore, the 2020 estimate was weak enough that chance can’t be ruled out as the explanation. Searches for “cyclospora” were also lower and more scattered that year.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her about the smaller reaction, Yang pointed to timing. “Shoppers barely reacted until the recall came,” she remarked.

It has been revealed that “Once specific products were named, purchases dropped. 2020 was also the summer of COVID, and that likely pulled attention away from other health news.”.

The 2018 outbreaks cost about $79 million, roughly 1.6 percent of a bagged salad market worth about $4.91 billion a year by the industry estimate the authors cite.

Recent findings suggest that yang’s earlier work put the retail cost of each of two salmonella outbreaks tied to onions above $1 billion. The authors attribute part of that gap to salmonella being a name that more shoppers recognize.

In a recent development, google searches catch people looking for information online and miss what they hear on TV, on the radio or from a neighbor. Regions that get their outbreak news offline may be underrepresented.

The search data also can’t show what any individual shopper read, so the results describe regions, not people.

The CDC records the date of a first illness, which comes before the public hears anything. So the study measured changes over whole outbreak-and-recall windows rather than the first days of alarm.

This year’s record, roughly 20,000 confirmed cyclospora cases by the CDC’s count, falls outside the study.

Yang said it raises the questions she would like to explore next: how the scale of the outbreak and the shifting information shaped what people bought.

Sources indicate that for a shopper standing in the produce aisle in the middle of one, she had plainer advice. “Follow the official alerts,” she said. “Early on, the source information is often unclear, so if you can’t tell where your salad came from, it’s fine to avoid it for a while.”.

According to recent reports, “Once a product is confirmed, check whether your salad is on the recall list,” Yang mentioned. “Washing won’t effectively remove the parasite.” Cooking, she added, kills it.

The full study was published in the journal Risk Analysis.

Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the dairy industry’s “Milk.
  • In a recent development, “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement.
  • To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

In a recent development, “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan said. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Sources indicate that women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

The authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

“Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” mentioned Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, newly introduced, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

Europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” mentioned Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept.
  • A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.
  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

According to recent reports, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

Sources indicate that “I know it’s going to be my main push,” he mentioned. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators mentioned. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., mentioned earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

Recent findings suggest that while ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how promptly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, remarked that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

According to recent reports, democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries noted.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks remarked. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#100517. Tiny changes in your pupil size and blinking rate reveal how hard your brain is working

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1016 w)

Tiny changes in your pupil size and blinking rate reveal how hard your brain is working

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.
  • Recent findings suggest that A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task indicates up in the eyes.
  • A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.

Recent findings suggest that A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task indicates up in the eyes. Pupils open wider and blinks come faster, and a VR headset with an eye tracker inside can record both.

A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard. The answer was mostly yes for healthy volunteers, and not yet for the patients.

Jordan Tsigarides of the University of East Anglia‘s School of Health Sciences led the study, which was part of his Ph.D., with colleagues at UEA and the University of Southampton.

Recent findings suggest that virtual reality is already used as a drug-free way to ease pain, he stated. His goal is a headset that changes what it shows, based on how a patient is coping.

“Imagine putting on a VR headset that can recognize when you’re becoming mentally tired or overwhelmed and automatically adjust the experience to suit you,” Tsigarides said in an interview with Earth.com.

“On a difficult day, it might simplify an activity or guide you through a calming environment.”.

In a recent development, the study tested only whether the headset could read the effort. It didn’t treat anyone’s pain.

Between March and June 2025, 84 adults put on a consumer VR headset with built-in eye tracking and played a memory game.

Half had lived with musculoskeletal pain for at least three months, most often rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis or fibromyalgia.

The other half were healthy university students and staff. They were younger on average, 35 years to the patients’ 58.

Letters appeared one at a time on a gray panel, each for three-quarters of a second. At the easiest level, a player pressed a button when a letter matched the one just before it. At the hardest, the match was four letters back. The whole session lasted under 20 minutes.

Players found it hard, and stated so. Their own ratings of effort kept climbing through the top level, even after their scores had stopped getting worse.

Pupils widened as the levels got harder, by about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) at most, which is less than the thickness of a credit card. Blinks came more often too.

Both changes revealed up in people with chronic pain and in people without it, and pain and fatigue scores made no difference to either one.

“What fascinated me was that people’s eyes responded to mental effort in remarkably similar ways, whether or not they lived with chronic pain,” Tsigarides told Earth.com.

Sources indicate that A plain average of pupil size told a computer almost nothing. A simple model that used average pupil size alone to sort the easiest level from the hardest guessed right 56 percent of the time in healthy volunteers.

According to recent reports, in patients it managed 51 percent, which is barely better than chance. The pattern was in the way the pupil changed second by second, not in its size.

Machine learning models that read the full, second-by-second trace did much better, at least in healthy volunteers. Tested on people they had never seen, the best models picked the easy level from the hard one with 88 percent accuracy.

In the chronic pain group, the same models managed 58 to 65 percent.

Age didn’t explain the gap. When the team matched volunteers and patients by age, or adjusted for it, the patients’ eyes were still harder to read.

The two groups also differed in education, medication and other illnesses, and the authors said a sample of 84 can’t untangle all of that.

It has been revealed that the patients were a varied group. Nearly all had two or more long-term conditions, and 45 percent took opioids. A quarter had dry eyes or another eye problem. None of those factors, on its own, predicted whose eyes the models misread.

“Rather than expecting one algorithm to work for everyone, we may need headsets that learn how each individual responds,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that one result was encouraging. People with chronic pain rated their motivation above 90 out of 100 at every level of the game, the same as the healthy group. Motion sickness scores were low in both groups, and pain scores didn’t rise during the session.

Tsigarides holds an honorary chief medical officer role at Revolve Labs Ltd, a company that helped fund his Ph.D. The paper discloses both.

Virtual reality for pain has so far been a fixed experience, Tsigarides said: everyone gets the same woodland walk or the same puzzle, however they feel that day.

His earlier work tested VR therapy in people with fibromyalgia, and he said this study is a step toward a version that adjusts itself.

Recent findings suggest that everyone was measured once, on one day. The researchers can’t say whether a patient’s eyes behave the same way on a good day and a bad one, and Tsigarides says investigating that question comes next.

“Someone’s ability to concentrate might be very different on a good day compared with a day when their pain or fatigue is particularly severe,” he noted.

The team also wants to move from a letter-matching game to the kind of calming scenes a real therapy uses, where changing light levels will complicate the pupil readings.

In a recent development, all of the models in this study were run afterward on a desktop computer rather than live inside the headset. None was tested on an outside group of patients.

It has been revealed that tsigarides told Earth.com he hopes early adaptive systems can be tested within a few years. Whether a headset that reads mental effort and responds to it actually eases anyone’s pain is a trial that hasn’t been run.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.
